cards.grammarNote:
**Hola** is used at any time of day, unlike English 'good morning/afternoon'
No abbreviated 'hi' equivalent — **hola** covers all casual greetings
The exclamation **¡** at the start is unique to Spanish punctuation

**por favor** literally means 'by favor' — a fixed phrase, always two words
Can be placed at the start or end of a request: **Por favor, dame el menú** or **Dame el menú, por favor**
**haz el favor** (do me the favor) is a more emphatic alternative

**gracias** is plural (literally 'thanks/graces') — always used in the plural form
**Muchas gracias** = thank you very much (many thanks)
From Latin *gratia* — related to English 'grace' and 'gratitude'

**De nada** literally means 'of nothing' — don't worry about it
Alternatives: **con mucho gusto** (with pleasure) · **no hay de qué** (there's nothing to thank for)
In Spain you may also hear **no hay problema** or simply **por favor**

Greetings by time of day:
**buenos días** (morning) · **buenas tardes** (afternoon/evening) · **buenas noches** (night)
Casually, just **buenas** works at any hour
cards.englishPhrase: Good morning! How did you sleep?

cards.grammarNote:
**buenas noches** is used both as a greeting and a farewell at night
**noches** is feminine plural — **buenas** agrees: **buenas** not *buenos*
**que duermas bien** (sleep well) uses the subjunctive — a soft wish or command

**¿Cómo estás?** uses **estar** (not **ser**) because it asks about a temporary state
**estás** = 2nd person singular informal · **está** = formal (usted)
Common responses: **bien** · **muy bien** · **más o menos** (so-so) · **mal** (not well)

**Mucho gusto** = 'much pleasure' — a set phrase used when first meeting someone
Also: **encantado** (masc.) / **encantada** (fem.) = delighted to meet you
Response: **igualmente** (likewise) or **el gusto es mío** (the pleasure is mine)
cards.englishPhrase: Nice to meet you, I'm Ana.

cards.grammarNote:
**adiós** = goodbye (final, like you may not see them again soon)
More casual farewells: **hasta luego** (see you later) · **hasta pronto** (see you soon) · **nos vemos** (see you)
**chao/chau** (from Italian *ciao*) is very common in Latin America

**perdón** = excuse me (apology or getting attention)
**con permiso** = excuse me (when passing someone or leaving)
**disculpe** = also common for getting a stranger's attention
cards.englishPhrase: Excuse me, where is the main street?

cards.grammarNote:
**lo siento** (I feel it) = I'm sorry
**perdón** → minor bumps or getting attention · **lo siento mucho** → genuine apologies
**querer** stem-changes e→ie: **yo quiero** · **tú quieres** · **él quiere**

**necesitar** is a regular -ar verb: **necesito · necesitas · necesita**
**Necesito** + infinitive = I need to do something: **Necesito ir** (I need to go)
Distinct from **querer** (to want) — stronger sense of requirement

**Me llamo** = 'I call myself' — from the reflexive verb **llamarse**
More natural in conversation than **mi nombre es**

Subject pronouns are often dropped — verb endings show who the subject is.
**Soy estudiante** and **Yo soy estudiante** are both correct — use **yo** for emphasis

Two forms of 'you': **tú** (informal, one person) · **usted** (formal)
**tú** → friends · **usted** → strangers, elders, formal settings
**usted** takes the same verb form as **él/ella**

**él** (he) has an accent mark to distinguish it from **el** (the)
Subject pronouns like **él/ella** are usually dropped in conversation — the verb ending makes the subject clear
**Él es** → often just **Es** unless you need to emphasize or clarify

**ella** (she) shares verb forms with **él** (he) and **usted** (formal you)
All three use the same conjugation: **trabaja, come, vive**
**ella** is typically dropped unless needed for emphasis or clarity

**nosotros** (masc. or mixed group) / **nosotras** (all-female group)
Spanish uses masculine plural as the default for mixed groups
**vosotros/vosotras** = you-all (Spain only) · **ustedes** = you-all (Latin America and formal Spain)

**ellos** (masc. or mixed) / **ellas** (all-female) — same masc. default rule as **nosotros**
Even one man in a group of women → **ellos**
**ellos/ellas** are usually dropped: **Comen juntos** is more natural than **Ellos comen juntos**

**mi** (my, singular) / **mis** (my, plural) — possessives agree in number, not gender
**mi amigo** · **mi amiga** · **mis amigos** · **mis amigas**
Note: **mi** has no accent; **mí** (with accent) means 'me' as an object of a preposition: **para mí** (for me)

**este** (masc.) / **esta** (fem.) for 'this' · **esto** = neutral, for unknown or abstract things
**¿Qué es esto?** (What is this?)

**ese** (masc.) / **esa** (fem.) = that (near the listener)
**aquel / aquella** = that over there (further away) — a three-way distance system
**eso / aquello** = neutral forms for unknown or abstract things

**muy** = very (before adjectives and adverbs): **muy bien** · **muy tarde** · **muy cansado**
Never use **muy** before a noun — use **mucho/a**: **mucho trabajo** (a lot of work)
**Está muy bien** uses **estar** — a temporary positive state, not a permanent definition

Spanish uses **tener** (to have) for hunger, thirst, and temperature:
**tengo hambre** (I'm hungry) · **tengo sed** (I'm thirsty) · **tengo frío/calor** (I'm cold/hot)
These are 'having' a feeling, not 'being' one

**sed** (thirst) is feminine: **tengo mucha sed**
Like **hambre** (hunger), it follows the **tener** pattern for physical states
**sed** also appears in the phrase **matar la sed** (to quench your thirst — literally 'kill the thirst')

**quién** (singular) / **quiénes** (plural) — always carries an accent in questions
**¿Quién es?** (Who is it?) · **¿Quiénes son?** (Who are they?)
Without accent, **quien** is a relative pronoun: **la persona quien habló** (the person who spoke)

**qué** (with accent) = what? in questions · **que** (no accent) = that, as a conjunction
**¿Qué quieres?** (What do you want?) vs **Sé que quieres** (I know that you want)
Also used in exclamations: **¡Qué bonito!** (How beautiful!)

**cuándo** (with accent) = when? in questions · **cuando** (no accent) = when, as a conjunction
**¿Cuándo llegas?** (When do you arrive?) vs **Llámame cuando llegues** (Call me when you arrive)
The conjunction triggers the subjunctive: **cuando llegues** not *cuando llegas*

**dónde** (with accent) = where? in questions · **donde** (no accent) = where, as a relative
**¿Dónde está el baño?** (Where is the bathroom?)
Location always takes **estar**: **¿Dónde está?** not *¿Dónde es?*

**por qué** (two words, accent) = why? · **porque** (one word, no accent) = because
**¿Por qué no vienes?** — **Porque estoy cansado.**

**cómo** (with accent) = how? in questions · **como** (no accent) = like/as, or 'I eat'
**¿Cómo estás?** (How are you?) · **como tú** (like you) · **como arroz** (I eat rice)
Also used for identity: **¿Cómo te llamas?** (What's your name?)

**ser** = permanent or defining traits: identity, origin, profession, material, time
**Soy americano** · **Es médico** · **Son las tres** (It's three o'clock)
When in doubt: is this a permanent fact about the subject?
cards.englishPhrase: I'm American and she's a doctor.
cards.phrase: Soy americano y ella es médica.

cards.grammarNote:
**estar** = temporary states, emotions, location, and progressive tenses
**Estoy cansado** · **Está en casa** · **Estamos comiendo**
Location always uses **estar** — even for permanent buildings
cards.englishPhrase: I'm tired and I'm at home.
cards.phrase: Estoy cansado y estoy en casa.

cards.grammarNote:
**tener** is irregular in yo: **tengo**
Also used for physical states: **tener hambre** (hungry) · **tener sed** (thirsty) · **tener frío/calor** (cold/hot)
cards.englishPhrase: I'm hungry. Do you have water?

cards.grammarNote:
**hacer** is irregular in yo: **hago**
Used in weather: **Hace calor** (It's hot) · **Hace frío** (It's cold)

**ir a** + infinitive = going to do something: **voy a comer** (I'm going to eat)
**a** + **el** → **al** (mandatory): **voy al mercado** (not *a el mercado*)

**venir** is irregular: **yo vengo** · **tú vienes** · **él viene**
**venir de** = to come from: **¿De dónde vienes?** (Where are you from?)

**comer** is the model regular -er verb: **como · comes · come · comemos · comen**
Meals can also be expressed as verbs: **desayunar** (to have breakfast) · **almorzar** (lunch) · **cenar** (dinner)
**¿Dónde comemos?** — subject pronoun dropped, nosotros implied by **-emos** ending
**poder** stem-changes o→ue: **yo puedo** · **tú puedes** · **él puede**

**decir** is irregular: **digo** · **dices** · **dice**
Command form: **dime** (tell me) · Appears in **¿Cómo se dice…?** and **quiero decir** (I mean)

**ver** is irregular in yo: **veo**
**A ver** (let's see) is one of the most common filler expressions in Spanish

**dar** is irregular in yo: **doy**
The command **dame** (give me) is extremely common: **Dame el menú** (Give me the menu)

**saber** = to know facts or how to do something: **¿Sabes nadar?** (Do you know how to swim?)
Irregular yo: **sé** · Not to be confused with **conocer**, which means to know people or places
cards.englishPhrase: Do you know what time it is?

cards.grammarNote:
**conocer** = to know / be familiar with people and places
**¿Conoces a María?** — notice the personal **a** before people
Irregular yo: **conozco**
cards.englishPhrase: Do you know a good restaurant here?

cards.grammarNote:
**hablar** is the model regular -ar verb:
**hablo · hablas · habla · hablamos · hablan**
Most -ar verbs follow this pattern exactly
**entender** stem-changes e→ie: **entiendo** · **entiendes** · **entiende**

**pensar** stem-changes e→ie: **yo pienso** · **tú piensas**
**Pienso que** and **creo que** both mean 'I think that' — **creo** is slightly more common in everyday speech

**gustar** works in reverse — the thing liked is the grammatical subject
**Me gusta el café** = coffee pleases me = I like coffee
Singular: **me gusta** · Plural: **me gustan** (e.g., **Me gustan los libros**)

**buscar** is a regular -ar verb but watch the spelling in preterite yo: **busqué** (not *buskei*) — c→qu before e to keep the hard /k/ sound
**buscar** doesn't need a separate 'for' — it's built into the verb: **Busco trabajo** (I'm looking for work)

**esperar** means both 'to wait' and 'to hope'
**Espera un momento** (wait a moment) · **Espero que sí** (I hope so)

**salir** is irregular in yo: **salgo**
**salir a** = to go out to: **¿Salimos a comer?** (Shall we go out to eat?)
**salir de** = to leave from: **Salgo del trabajo a las seis**
cards.englishPhrase: At what time does the bus leave?

cards.grammarNote:
**volver** stem-changes o→ue: **vuelvo** · **vuelves** · **vuelve**
**volver a** + infinitive = to do something again: **vuelvo a intentarlo** (I'll try again)

**llegar** is regular but has a spelling change in preterite yo: **llegué** (g→gu before e)
**llegar a** = to arrive at: **Llego a las ocho** (I arrive at eight)
Also used in **llegar tarde/temprano** (to arrive late/early) — very common expressions

**mirar** = to look at / watch (directs attention, implies observation)
**ver** = to see (more passive, just perceiving)
**¡Mira!** (informal) / **¡Mire!** (formal) — common attention-getters, like 'look!' or 'see!'
Don't confuse with **buscar** (to look for) — completely different meaning

Two words for 'but': **pero** (introduces a contrasting fact) · **sino** (introduces a correction: not X, *but rather* Y)
**No quiero café, sino té** (I don't want coffee, but tea)
**pero** is by far the more common and versatile of the two
cards.englishPhrase: I want to go, but I can't.

cards.grammarNote:
**y** → **e** before words starting with i or hi: **madre e hija** (mother and daughter)
**o** → **u** before words starting with o or ho: **siete u ocho** (seven or eight)

**o** → **u** before words starting with o or ho to avoid confusion: **uno u otro** (one or the other)
**o...o** = either...or: **o café o té** (either coffee or tea)
**ni...ni** = neither...nor: **ni café ni té** (neither coffee nor tea)

**porque** (one word, no accent) = because · **por qué** (two words, accent) = why?
**¿Por qué no vienes?** — **Porque estoy cansado.**
Easy trick: the question form has the accent
cards.englishPhrase: I can't come because I'm tired.
cards.phrase: No puedo venir porque estoy cansado.

cards.grammarNote:
**con** + **mí** → **conmigo** (with me) — a special fused form
**con** + **ti** → **contigo** (with you) — same fusion
**con** + **él/ella/usted** stays separate: **con él** (with him)
**Vine con mi amigo** — **vine** is the preterite of **venir**: yo vine (I came)

**sin** + infinitive is common: **sin saber** (without knowing) · **sin querer** (unintentionally — lit. 'without wanting to')
**sin** is the opposite of **con** — both are prepositions
**azúcar** (sugar) can be masculine or feminine depending on region: **el azúcar** or **la azúcar**

**para** = purpose or destination: **un regalo para ti** (a gift for you)
**por** = cause, exchange, duration: **gracias por tu ayuda** · **por dos horas** (for two hours)
cards.englishPhrase: This is for you. Thanks for everything.
cards.phrase: Esto es para ti. Gracias por todo.

cards.grammarNote:
**en** covers 'in', 'on', and 'at' in Spanish — context determines which
**en la mesa** (on the table) · **en casa** (at home) · **en México** (in Mexico)
**en** + transport: **en autobús** (by bus) · **en avión** (by plane) · **a pie** (on foot — exception)
cards.englishPhrase: The book is on the table.
cards.phrase: El libro está en la mesa.

cards.grammarNote:
**de** is one of the most common Spanish words
**de** + **el** → **del** (required): **el libro del maestro** (the teacher's book)
Used for origin, possession, and material

**hoy** = today · **ayer** = yesterday · **mañana** = tomorrow
**hoy en día** = nowadays (a fixed phrase)
Time adverbs in Spanish come after the verb: **¿Qué hacemos hoy?** — **hoy** at the end is natural

**mañana** has two meanings: tomorrow and morning
**Hasta mañana** = see you tomorrow · **por la mañana** = in the morning
**la mañana** (with article) = the morning · **mañana** alone = tomorrow

**ahora** = now · **ahora mismo** = right now (more emphatic)
**ahorita** is a diminutive form common in Mexico and Central America — it can mean 'right now', 'in a moment', or 'soon', depending on context
**ya** (already/now) overlaps with **ahora** in some uses: **¡ya voy!** (I'm coming now!)

**Hasta luego** = goodbye (literally: until later)
**luego** can also mean 'then' in a sequence: **Primero como, luego descanso** (First I eat, then I rest)

**también** = also/too (affirmative) · **tampoco** = neither/not either (negative)
**Yo también** = me too · **Yo tampoco** = me neither
**¿Y tú?** / **¿Y usted?** = And you? — a natural follow-up after stating your own view

**tal vez** and **quizás** both mean 'maybe'
**Tal vez venga** (subjunctive — more uncertain) · **Tal vez viene** (indicative — more certain)

**siempre** = always · **nunca** = never · **a veces** = sometimes · **normalmente** = normally
**tomar** here means to drink — **tomar** is used more broadly than **beber** in Latin America
**por la mañana** = in the morning (lit. 'through/by the morning')
cards.englishPhrase: I always drink coffee in the morning.
cards.phrase: Siempre tomo café por la mañana.

cards.grammarNote:
**nunca** usually comes before the verb: **Nunca llego tarde**
If placed after, add **no** before the verb: **no llego tarde nunca**
Unlike English, double negatives are grammatically correct in Spanish

**más** = more · **menos** = less · **más o menos** = so-so / more or less
**más** + adjective = comparative: **más grande** (bigger) · **más tarde** (later)
**más** has an accent to distinguish it from **mas** (an old literary word for 'but')

**mucho** before a noun: agrees in gender/number — **mucho trabajo** · **mucha agua** · **muchos amigos** · **muchas gracias**
**mucho** after a verb (as adverb): invariable — **Trabajo mucho** (I work a lot)
**muy** is used before adjectives/adverbs: **muy bueno** (very good) — never *mucho bueno*
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of work.

cards.grammarNote:
**un poco** = a little (used before **de** + noun or before adverbs)
**un poco de agua** (a little water) · **un poco cansado** (a little tired)
**poquito** is the diminutive — a very small amount, or used to soften a request: **un poquito más** (just a tiny bit more)
cards.phrase: Un poco de agua, por favor.

cards.grammarNote:
**persona** is feminine regardless of the person's gender — **una persona simpática** even if the person is male
The personal **a** is required before a specific person as a direct object: **Veo a una persona** (I see a person)

**lugar** is masculine: **un buen lugar** · **el lugar**
**sitio** is a common synonym: **un buen sitio**
**lugar** also appears in the idiom **en lugar de** (instead of)
cards.englishPhrase: Do you know a good place?

cards.grammarNote:
**cosa** is feminine: **una cosa** · **la cosa**
Used in many common phrases: **ninguna cosa** → usually contracted to **nada** (nothing)
**¿Qué es esa cosa?** — **esa** (fem.) agrees with **cosa** (fem.)

Three levels of 'here/there' in Spanish:
**aquí** (here, near me) · **ahí** (there, near you) · **allí/allá** (there, far from both)
**Ven aquí** = Come here · **Está ahí** = It's there (near you) · **Está allá** = It's over there

**allí** = there (specific location) · **allá** = over there (more vague or further)
**ahí** = there near the listener
**hay** (there is/are) sounds like 'ai' — completely unrelated: **Hay un baño allí** (There is a bathroom there)

**agua** is feminine but takes **el** in the singular (begins with stressed 'a')
Adjectives still agree feminine: **el agua fría** · Plural: **las aguas**
cards.phrase: Un vaso de agua, por favor.

cards.grammarNote:
Use **estar** (not **ser**) with food quality adjectives — they are temporary states
**La comida está deliciosa** ✓ · **ser** would imply a permanent quality, which sounds odd for food

**casa** is feminine: **la casa** · **mi casa**
**en casa** (at home) is used without an article — a fixed expression
**ser** vs **estar**: **La casa es grande** (the house is big — permanent trait) vs **La casa está cerca** (the house is nearby — location always uses **estar**)

**tienda** = store/shop (general) — feminine: **la tienda**
**La tienda está cerrada** uses **estar** — **cerrada** (closed) is a state, not a permanent trait
Compare: **La tienda es nueva** (the store is new — permanent characteristic) vs **está cerrada** (currently closed — temporary state)

**efectivo** = cash (literally 'effective/actual money')
**tarjeta** = card · **tarjeta de crédito** (credit card) · **tarjeta de débito** (debit card)
In Spain: **metálico** is another word for cash

**ayuda** = help (noun, feminine) · **ayudar** = to help (verb)
**Necesito tu ayuda** — note **tu** (your, no accent) vs **tú** (you, with accent)
**¡Ayuda!** alone = Help! (emergency cry)

**baño** = bathroom/toilet (masculine)
Regional terms: **servicio** or **aseo** (Spain) · **baño** is understood everywhere
Location always takes **estar**: **¿Dónde está el baño?** — never **¿Dónde es?**

**bueno** shortens to **buen** before masculine nouns: **un buen día** (a good day)
**Buenas** alone is a casual greeting at any time of day

**malo** shortens to **mal** before masculine nouns: **un mal día** (a bad day)
Also used in **estar mal** (to feel bad, to be wrong)

**grande** shortens to **gran** before any noun (masc. or fem.): **un gran hombre** · **una gran idea**
**gran** often implies greatness, not just size

**pequeño** (masc.) / **pequeña** (fem.) — adjectives agree with the noun they describe
**Una mesa pequeña** — adjective follows the noun (most Spanish adjectives come after)
Diminutive **-ito/-ita** can replace small: **mesita** (little table) · **momentito** (just a moment)

**listo** with **estar** = ready: **Estoy listo** (I'm ready)
**listo** with **ser** = clever/smart: **Es muy listo** (He's very clever) — same word, different meaning depending on ser/estar!
**listo/lista** agrees with gender: **¿Estás lista?** (Are you ready? — to a woman)

**cansado** uses **estar** (not **ser**) — tiredness is a temporary state
**cansado/cansada** agrees with the subject's gender: **Estoy cansado** (masc.) · **Estoy cansada** (fem.)
Past participle used as adjective: from the verb **cansar** (to tire/wear out)

**ayudarme** = help me — the object pronoun **me** attaches to the infinitive
Alternatively, it can come before the conjugated verb: **¿Me puedes ayudar?** — both are correct
**Perdón** at the start softens the request — polite attention-getter before asking for help
cards.englishPhrase: Excuse me, can you help me find the station?
cards.phrase: Perdón, ¿puedes ayudarme a encontrar la estación?

cards.grammarNote:
**costar** is an o→ue stem-changing verb: **cuesta** (it costs) · **cuestan** (they cost)
**¿Cuánto cuesta?** = singular item · **¿Cuánto cuestan?** = multiple items
**¿Cuánto** agrees with context: **¿Cuánto es?** is also common at a checkout
cards.englishPhrase: How much does this shirt cost?

cards.grammarNote:
**la cuenta** = the bill/check at a restaurant (feminine)
To ask for it: **La cuenta, por favor** or **¿Me trae la cuenta?** (Can you bring me the bill?)
**cuenta** also means 'account' (bank account) and appears in **darse cuenta de** (to realize something)

**menú** is a loanword from French — note the accent on the final syllable
**la carta** is another word for menu, especially common in Spain
**¿Me das el menú?** — literally 'Do you give me the menu?' — a natural informal request

**mesa** is feminine: **la mesa** · **una mesa**
**Una mesa para dos** = a table for two — **para** here expresses purpose/destination
In a restaurant: **¿Tienen mesa para dos?** (Do you have a table for two?)
cards.phrase: Una mesa para dos, por favor.

cards.grammarNote:
**saber** is highly irregular in yo: **sé** (just one letter, with accent to distinguish from **se** the reflexive pronoun)
**saber** = to know facts · **conocer** = to know people/places
**No sé** is one of the most natural responses in any conversation
cards.englishPhrase: I don't know where it is.

cards.grammarNote:
**agua** is feminine but takes **el** in the singular (starts with stressed 'a')
Adjectives still agree feminine: **el agua fría** (cold water) · Plural: **las aguas**

**pan** is masculine: **el pan** · **Quisiera** is the imperfect subjunctive of **querer** used as a polite 'I would like' — softer than **quiero** (I want)
Common in restaurants throughout the Spanish-speaking world

**arroz** is masculine: **el arroz** · Comes from Arabic **al-ruzz** — one of many Arabic food words in Spanish
**Me gusta** (it pleases me) is how Spanish expresses liking: the thing liked is the grammatical subject, so singular items use **gusta** and plural items use **gustan**: **me gustan las verduras**
cards.phrase: Me gusta el arroz con verduras.

cards.grammarNote:
**leche** is feminine: **la leche** · **¿Quieres?** is the tú (informal) form of **querer** — an e→ie stem-changing verb
Full present: **quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, queréis, quieren**

**huevo** is masculine: **el huevo**, plural **los huevos** · **desayuno** doubles as both the noun (breakfast) and the yo-form verb **desayunar** (to have breakfast)
**Como** (I eat) is the yo form of **comer** — a regular -er verb: como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen
cards.englishPhrase: I eat two eggs for breakfast.
cards.phrase: Como dos huevos en el desayuno.

cards.grammarNote:
**queso** is masculine: **el queso** · **sándwich** is an English borrowing fully adopted into Spanish, written with an accent: **el sándwich**
**tiene** is the él/ella form of **tener** (to have): tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen

**pollo** is masculine: **el pollo** · **está delicioso** uses **estar** rather than **ser** because food quality is a temporary, subjective condition
Compare: **La manzana es verde** (ser — inherent color) vs **La sopa está caliente** (estar — current temperature)

**carne** is feminine: **la carne** · The subject pronoun **Él** (he) is optional in Spanish — it is included here for emphasis or clarity
Note: **él** (he) carries an accent to distinguish it from **el** (the)

**pescado** (cooked/caught fish, food) vs **pez** (live fish in water) — the same distinction as English 'fish (to eat)' vs 'fish (the animal)'
**pescado** is masculine: **el pescado**

**fruta** is feminine: **la fruta** (uncountable, as a category) · Individual pieces: **una fruta** (a piece of fruit)
**todos los días** = every day — literally 'all the days'; **día** is masculine despite ending in -a: **el día**

**manzana** is feminine: **la manzana** · Also means 'city block' in Latin America — context distinguishes the two meanings
**al día** = per day / a day — **al** is the contraction of **a + el**
cards.englishPhrase: An apple a day is healthy.
cards.phrase: Una manzana al día es saludable.

cards.grammarNote:
**café** is masculine: **el café** · From Arabic **qahwa** → Turkish **kahve** → Spanish **café**
Diminutive of affection: **cafecito** — very common in Latin America, used to warmly offer coffee: **¿Un cafecito?**
**por la mañana** = in the morning; also: **por la tarde** (in the afternoon), **por la noche** (in the evening/at night)
cards.englishPhrase: I like coffee in the morning.
cards.phrase: Me gusta el café por la mañana.

cards.grammarNote:
**té** is masculine: **el té** · Written with an accent to distinguish it from **te** (the indirect object pronoun 'you/to you')
**¿Quieres un té?** — note the indefinite article **un** before **té**; in English we often omit the article ('some tea'), but Spanish commonly uses **un/una**

**vino** is masculine: **el vino** · Color terms for wine differ from English: **vino tinto** (red wine — literally 'dyed/tinted wine'), **vino blanco** (white wine), **vino rosado** (rosé)
**copa** = wine glass (stemmed glass); **vaso** = regular drinking glass — use **copa** for wine, **vaso** for water/juice
cards.englishPhrase: A glass of red wine, please.
cards.phrase: Una copa de vino tinto, por favor.

cards.grammarNote:
**cerveza** is feminine: **la cerveza** · From Latin **cervesia** — a Gaulish/Celtic word that entered Latin
In Spain, a small beer on tap is called a **caña**; a larger glass is a **jarra** · In Latin America ordering **una chela** (informal) is common in Mexico

**azúcar** from Arabic **al-sukkar** (itself from Sanskrit **śarkarā**) — one of the clearest Arabic food etymologies in Spanish
**azúcar** is unusual: it is used with both **el** and **la** — **el azúcar** is more common in Spain, **la azúcar** in parts of Latin America
**sin** = without — used before a noun with no article: **sin azúcar** (no sugar), **sin sal** (no salt), **sin leche** (no milk)

**sal** is feminine: **la sal** · **¿Me pasas la sal?** is an indirect request using the present tense — more natural in Spanish than the English-style 'could you pass?'
The indirect object pronoun **me** (to me) is placed before the conjugated verb

**comer** is a regular -er verb: **como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen**
**¡Vamos a comer!** — **vamos a + infinitive** = let's [do something] (also functions as near future: 'we are going to eat')
**comer** can be used as a noun with the article: **la comida** or informally **el comer**: **El comer sano es importante**

**beber** is a regular -er verb: **bebo, bebes, bebe, bebemos, bebéis, beben**
Synonym: **tomar** (to take/drink) — widely used for beverages: **tomar agua**, **tomar café**; **beber** is slightly more formal/literary
**algo de beber** = something to drink — **algo de + infinitive** = something to [do]
cards.englishPhrase: Would you like something to drink?

cards.grammarNote:
Use **tener** (to have) for hunger, thirst, and other physical states:
**tener hambre** (hungry) · **tener sed** (thirsty) · **tener frío/calor** (cold/hot) · **tener miedo** (afraid) · **tener sueño** (sleepy)
These are expressed with **tener**, not **estar**

**sed** (thirst) is feminine: **la sed** — though the article is rarely used in the **tener sed** construction
**el hambre** and **la sed** are both feminine nouns used in the same pattern: **tener hambre/sed** (to be hungry/thirsty — literally 'to have hunger/thirst')
Note the gender surprise: **el hambre** is actually feminine — it uses **el** only to avoid the vowel clash **la hambre → el hambre**

**desayuno** is masculine: **el desayuno** · From **des-** (un-) + **ayuno** (fast) — 'breaking the fast,' just like English 'breakfast'
**Desayuno** (I have breakfast) — the verb **desayunar** is also regular: desayuno, desayunas, desayuna…
**a las siete** = at seven — times use **a la/las** (at one o'clock: **a la una**; other hours: **a las dos/tres**…)

**almuerzo** is masculine: **el almuerzo** · **almorzar** (to have lunch) is an o→ue stem-changing verb: **almuerzo, almuerzas, almuerza, almorzamos, almorzáis, almuerzan**
In Spain, **la comida** (the meal) typically refers to lunch — the main meal of the day, eaten around 2–3 pm

**cena** is feminine: **la cena** · **cenar** = to have dinner (regular -ar verb)
**está lista** — **estar** for the current state (readiness) and **lista** agrees feminine with **la cena**
In Spain dinner (**la cena**) is typically light and eaten late, around 9–10 pm

**cerdo** is masculine: **el cerdo** · Also means 'pig' (the animal) — context makes the meaning clear
In Spain, **jamón** (cured ham from pork) is central to culinary culture; **jamón ibérico** and **jamón serrano** are famous regional varieties

**plátano** is masculine: **el plátano** · Regional variation: in many Latin American countries the word **banano** or **banana** is preferred for the sweet fruit; **plátano** may specifically mean the larger cooking plantain
**maduros** (ripe) — adjective agrees masculine plural with **plátanos**: maduro → maduros

**naranja** is feminine: **la naranja** · Etymology: from Sanskrit **nāranga** → Persian → Arabic **nāranja** → Spanish **naranja** — a classic Arabic food borrowing
In Latin America **jugo** = juice; in Spain **zumo** is more common: **zumo de naranja**
Diminutive of affection: **naranjita** (little orange / dear orange)

**verdura** is feminine: **la verdura** · Comes from **verde** (green) — originally meant 'green things'
Also common: **vegetal** or **hortaliza** for individual vegetables · **¡Come las verduras!** is a tú imperative (informal command): the tú imperative of -er verbs uses the él/ella form: **come** (from comer)

**papa** is feminine: **la papa** (used throughout Latin America) · In Spain: **patata** — same vegetable, different word
Both come from Quechua **papa** — the potato is native to the Andes
**puré de papas** (mashed potatoes) — **puré** is masculine: **el puré**

**tomate** is masculine: **el tomate** · From Nahuatl **tomatl** — a word borrowed into Spanish during the colonial period
**ensalada** is feminine: **la ensalada** · **tiene** = has (él/ella form of **tener**)

**cebolla** is feminine: **la cebolla** · **No me gustan** — note the verb is plural (**gustan**) because the subject is **las cebollas** (plural)
With **gustar**, the verb agrees with what is liked, not the person: **me gusta el café** but **me gustan las cebollas**

**ensalada** is feminine: **la ensalada** · From **sal** (salt) — originally 'salted greens'
**Voy a tomar** uses **ir a + infinitive** for the near future: 'I'm going to have…'
**tomar** literally means 'to take' but is widely used for eating/drinking: **tomar un café**, **tomar una ensalada**

**sopa** is feminine: **la sopa** · **está caliente** uses **estar** (not **ser**) for the temporary state of being hot — food temperature is always expressed with **estar**
Diminutive: **sopita** (a nice little soup / soup served affectionately)

**sándwich** is an English borrowing: **el sándwich** — note the written accent on the first syllable following Spanish stress rules
In Mexico a long sandwich roll is called a **torta**; in Cuba **medianoche** or **pan con** varieties are common — regional vocabulary varies widely
**Hice** is the irregular preterite (past tense) yo form of **hacer** (to make/do): hice, hiciste, hizo, hicimos, hicisteis, hicieron
cards.englishPhrase: I made a sandwich for lunch.
cards.phrase: Hice un sándwich para el almuerzo.

cards.grammarNote:
**jugo** is masculine: **el jugo** · Used throughout Latin America; in Spain the preferred word is **zumo**: **zumo de naranja**
Diminutive: **jugito** — used affectionately, especially when offering juice to children: **¿Quieres un jugito?**

**cocinar** is a regular -ar verb: **cocino, cocinas, cocina, cocinamos, cocináis, cocinan**
The person who cooks is **el/la cocinero/a** (cook/chef); a more skilled chef: **el/la chef** (borrowed from French)
**cocina muy bien** — adverbs like **bien** (well) and **mal** (badly) don't change form

**comida** is feminine: **la comida** · From **comer** (to eat) — literally 'what is eaten'
**comida** has multiple meanings: food in general, a meal, or specifically lunch (in Spain)
**Esta es una comida deliciosa** — note **deliciosa** agrees feminine with **comida**

**menú** is masculine: **el menú** · Written with an accent on the **ú** — borrowed from French **menu**
**¿Puedo ver…?** = Can I see…? — **poder** (can/to be able) is an o→ue stem-changing verb: **puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden**
Also common in restaurants: **la carta** = the menu (the physical card listing dishes)

**restaurante** is masculine: **el restaurante** · From French **restaurant** ('restoring') — the original French restaurants advertised 'restorative broths'
**está bien** uses **estar** for a current quality (how things are going) rather than **es bueno** (ser) which would state an inherent permanent characteristic

**camarero** (masculine) / **camarera** (feminine) = waiter/waitress · Primarily used in Spain
Regional alternatives: **mesero/mesera** (Mexico, Colombia), **mozo/moza** (Argentina, Peru), **garzón** (Chile)
**la cuenta** (the bill/check) is feminine: remember to say **¿Me trae la cuenta?** (Can you bring me the bill?)

**mesa** is feminine: **la mesa** · From Latin **mensa** (table, also altar)
**Nuestra mesa está lista** — **nuestra** (our) is a possessive adjective agreeing feminine with **mesa**: nuestro/nuestra, vuestro/vuestra
**está lista** — **lista** (ready) agrees feminine here; note **lista** also means 'list' and 'clever'

**plato** is masculine: **el plato** · **plato** also means 'dish' (a prepared food item): **el plato del día** (dish of the day), **un plato de pasta** (a plate of pasta)
**está sucio** — **estar** for condition; **sucio** (dirty) agrees masculine with **plato**

**vaso** is masculine: **el vaso** · **vaso** = everyday drinking glass; **copa** = stemmed glass (wine, champagne)
**un vaso de agua** — the construction **un/una [container] de [contents]** is the standard way to order drinks: **un vaso de agua**, **una taza de café**, **una copa de vino**
cards.phrase: Un vaso de agua, por favor.

cards.grammarNote:
**botella** is feminine: **la botella** · From Old French **boteille** (bottle)
**una botella de vino** — same [container] de [contents] pattern · Useful in restaurants: **una botella de agua mineral** (a bottle of mineral water), **con gas** (sparkling) or **sin gas** (still)
cards.phrase: Una botella de vino, por favor.

cards.grammarNote:
**pastel** is masculine: **el pastel** · In Mexico and Central America **pastel** = cake; in Spain **tarta** is more common for layer cakes
**pastel** also means 'pastel (color)' and 'pie' depending on context — a versatile word!

**galleta** is feminine: **la galleta** · **galleta** covers both cookies (sweet) and crackers (savory) — context or a modifier clarifies: **galleta salada** (cracker), **galleta dulce** (sweet cookie)
**estas galletas** — **estas** is the feminine plural demonstrative: esta → estas (this/these)

**chocolate** is masculine: **el chocolate** · From Nahuatl **xocolātl** (bitter water) — brought to Europe from Mesoamerica in the 16th century
**Me encanta** = I love it (literally 'it enchants me') — **encantar** works exactly like **gustar**: the thing loved is the grammatical subject

**mantequilla** is feminine: **la mantequilla** · From **manteca** (lard/fat) + diminutive **-illa** — literally 'little fat'
In Spain **mantequilla** = butter; **manteca** = lard · In Argentina **manteca** can mean butter
**Pongo** is the irregular yo form of **poner** (to put): pongo, pones, pone, ponemos, ponéis, ponen
cards.englishPhrase: I put butter on my bread.

cards.grammarNote:
**aceite** is masculine: **el aceite** · From Arabic **az-zayt** (the olive oil) — another key Arabic culinary borrowing
Spain is one of the world's largest olive oil producers; **aceite de oliva virgen extra** (extra virgin olive oil) is a staple
**oliva** = the olive (fruit/tree); **aceituna** is the more common word for the olive you eat

**pimienta** is feminine: **la pimienta** · Refers to ground black/white pepper (the spice)
Distinguish from **pimiento** (masculine: **el pimiento**) = bell pepper or chile pepper — the vegetable
From Latin **pigmentum** (pigment, substance) via medieval cooking vocabulary

**cocina** is feminine: **la cocina** · **cocina** is a versatile word: it means 'kitchen' (the room), 'stove/cooker' (the appliance), and is also the él/ella/usted form of **cocinar** (to cook)
**está limpia** — **estar** for condition; **limpia** (clean) agrees feminine with **cocina**

**horno** is masculine: **el horno** · **al horno** = baked/roasted (in the oven): **pollo al horno** (roast chicken), **papas al horno** (baked potatoes)
From Latin **furnus** — the Spanish word underwent sound change f→h at the start of words (also: **farina** → **harina**, **filium** → **hijo**)

**estufa** is feminine: **la estufa** · In Latin America **estufa** = kitchen stove/cooker; in Spain the stove/hob is usually **la cocina** or **los fogones**
**Cocínalo** is a command (tú imperative) with a direct object pronoun attached: **cocina + lo** (cook + it) — pronouns attach to the end of affirmative commands

**cuchillo** is masculine: **el cuchillo** · Related to **cuchilla** (blade) and **cuchara** (spoon) — all from Latin **cochlearium** (ladle/spoon), which spawned a family of eating utensil words
**afilado** (sharp) agrees masculine with **cuchillo** — feminine would be **afilada**

**tenedor** is masculine: **el tenedor** · From **tener** (to hold/have) — literally 'the holder'
**¿Me da un tenedor?** uses the usted form **da** (gives) — polite register appropriate for asking a waiter
Compare tú form: **¿Me das un tenedor?** (more informal)

**cuchara** is feminine: **la cuchara** · Diminutive **cucharita** = teaspoon; **cucharada** = a spoonful (a common unit in recipes)
**cucharón** (augmentative) = a large ladle/serving spoon — Spanish uses suffixes to indicate size: -ito/-ita (small), -ón/-ona (large)

**hornear** (to bake) comes from **horno** (oven) — a regular -ar verb
Alternative: **cocer al horno** (to cook in the oven) is also common
**los domingos** = on Sundays (every Sunday) — using the plural definite article with a day of the week expresses habitual action

**freír** is an e→i stem-changing verb (like **pedir**): **frío, fríes, fríe, freímos, freís, fríen**
Note the written accent on **fríe** (command/present) to distinguish it from **frie** (uncommon)
**sofreír** = to sauté (lightly fry) — a useful cooking verb

**mezclar** is a regular -ar verb · **mezcla** = the mix/mixture (noun, feminine)
**Mezcla todos los ingredientes** — **mezcla** is both the tú imperative and the él/ella present tense form (context distinguishes them)
**todos los ingredientes** — **todos** (all/every, masculine plural) agrees with the masculine plural **ingredientes**

**verter** is an e→ie stem-changing verb: **vierto, viertes, vierte, vertemos, vertéis, vierten**
Alternative: **echar** is the everyday word for pouring/adding liquids in cooking: **échale agua** (pour in some water)
**Vierte el agua en el vaso** — note **el agua** (feminine noun with masculine article for vowel harmony)
cards.englishPhrase: Pour the water into the glass.
cards.phrase: Vierte el agua en el vaso.

cards.grammarNote:
**servir** is an e→i stem-changing verb (same pattern as **pedir**): **sirvo, sirves, sirve, servimos, servís, sirven**
**sirvió** is the él/ella preterite (past) form — note the e→i stem change carries into the preterite for -ir verbs: sirvió, sirvieron
**servir** also means 'to be useful': **¿Para qué sirve?** (What is it good for?)

**fresco** is an adjective that changes for gender and number: **fresco** (m. sg.), **fresca** (f. sg.), **frescos** (m. pl.), **frescas** (f. pl.)
**El pan está fresco** — **estar** for current condition (freshness is temporary)
**fresco** also means 'cool' (weather): **Está fresco afuera** (It's cool outside)

**cocido** is the past participle of **cocer** (to cook/boil), used here as an adjective
As an adjective it must agree: **cocido/cocida/cocidos/cocidas** — here **cocido** agrees masculine with **el pollo**
**¿Está cocido el pollo?** — **estar** for the current state; the subject (**el pollo**) comes after the verb (common in questions and when adding emphasis)

Use **estar** for food and drink temperatures — they are temporary states
**La sopa está caliente** · **El café está frío**
Compare with **ser** for inherent qualities: **El chile es picante** (chili is always spicy)
cards.englishPhrase: Be careful, the soup is hot.

cards.grammarNote:
**frío** (cold) changes for gender: **frío/fría/fríos/frías**
**Mi café está frío** — **estar** for the temporary condition of being cold
**frío** is also the noun: **el frío** (the cold); **tener frío** = to be cold (of a person): **Tengo frío** (I'm cold) — same **tener** pattern as hunger and thirst

**dulce** doesn't change for gender (same ending for masculine and feminine): **el café dulce**, **la limonada dulce**
**Este pastel está muy dulce** — **estar** for the current subjective taste experience
**dulce** is also a noun: **el dulce** = candy/sweet treat, especially in Mexico and Central America · **los dulces** = candies

**picante** doesn't change for gender: **el chile picante**, **la salsa picante**
**suele ser picante** — **soler + infinitive** means 'to usually do' (habitual action): **suelo comer** (I usually eat)
**ser** (not **estar**) because spiciness is an inherent characteristic of Mexican food — compare with **La sopa está caliente** (temporary state) vs **El chile es picante** (permanent trait)
cards.phrase: La comida mexicana suele ser picante.

cards.grammarNote:
**delicioso** changes for gender: **delicioso/deliciosa/deliciosos/deliciosas**
**¡Esto está delicioso!** — **esto** (this) is a neuter demonstrative used when the item hasn't been specified or is abstract · **está** (not **es**) because deliciousness is a subjective sensory experience
Alternatives for 'delicious': **riquísimo** (super tasty), **buenísimo** (really good), **¡qué rico!** (how tasty!)

**saludable** doesn't change for gender: **el desayuno saludable**, **la comida saludable**
**La fruta es saludable** — **ser** (not estar) because healthiness is an inherent characteristic, not a temporary state
Related words: **la salud** (health), **sano/sana** (healthy, as an adjective for people and food — more colloquial than **saludable**)

**vegetariano/vegetariana** — the adjective agrees with the person: a woman says **Soy vegetariana**
**Soy** (I am, from **ser**) is used for identity and defining characteristics — being vegetarian is a permanent choice/identity, so **ser** is correct
Note: **¿Hay opciones vegetarianas?** (Are there vegetarian options?) — useful restaurant phrase

**Voy a casa** (I'm going home) — notice no article before **casa** in this fixed phrase, unlike other destinations: **voy a la escuela**, **voy al banco**.
**Casa** is feminine: **la casa**. Used for the concept of 'home' as much as the physical building.

**Vivo en** (I live in) uses **en** because you are located there, not travelling there.
Contrast: **Voy a un apartamento** (I'm going to an apartment) vs **Vivo en un apartamento** (I live in an apartment).
Alternative word in Spain: **el piso** (literally 'floor/storey').

**La escuela** is feminine — use **la** (the) and **una** (a).
**Van a la escuela** — going to a place uses **ir a**: **voy a la escuela**, **vamos al mercado**.
**Los niños** = the children (masculine plural covers mixed or all-male groups). Feminine: **las niñas**.
cards.phrase: Los niños van a la escuela.

cards.grammarNote:
**La universidad** is feminine despite ending in **-dad** (all **-dad** nouns are feminine: la ciudad, la libertad, la identidad).
**Estudia en la universidad** — use **en** for being/studying at a location.
The phrase uses **ella** (she) explicitly, which is optional in Spanish since the verb ending already signals the subject.

**La oficina** is feminine — **la** / **una oficina**.
**Trabaja en una oficina** — use **en** for location (working at/in a place).
Compare: **Voy a la oficina** (I'm going to the office — direction) vs **Estoy en la oficina** (I'm at the office — location).
**Él** (he) includes an accent mark to distinguish it from **el** (the).

**a** + **el** → **al** · **de** + **el** → **del** (mandatory contractions)
**Voy al hospital** (not *a el*) · **Vengo del banco** (not *de el*)
**El hospital** from Latin **hospes** (host/guest) — same root as **hotel**, **hostal**, **hostelería**, and English *hospitality*.
**El** hospital — masculine gender.

**Necesito ir al supermercado** — **al** = **a + el** (mandatory contraction before a masculine noun).
**La tienda de abarrotes** is the Latin American term; Spain uses **la tienda de comestibles** or simply **el supermercado**.
**Necesito + infinitive** = I need to [do something]: **necesito ir**, **necesito comprar**, **necesito salir**.
cards.englishPhrase: I need to go to the supermarket.

cards.grammarNote:
**Del** = **de + el** — mandatory contraction. **Vengo del banco** (I'm coming from the bank).
**El banco** is masculine. Note: **banco** also means *bench* — context tells them apart.
**Vengo de** = I'm coming from. Compare: **Voy al banco** (going to) vs **Vengo del banco** (coming from).

**La biblioteca** — feminine noun, from Greek **biblion** (book) + **theke** (storage/case). The same root gives English *bibliography* and *Bible*.
**Estudio en la biblioteca** — use **en** for location (being/studying there), not **a**: **en** = at/in, **a** = to (direction).
Don't confuse with **la librería** = bookshop (a *false friend* — librería is NOT library).

**El restaurante** is masculine — **el** / **un restaurante**.
**Está lleno** uses **estar** (not **ser**) because fullness is a temporary state. Compare: **El restaurante es famoso** (permanent quality — it's famous) vs **El restaurante está lleno** (temporary — it's full right now).
**Lleno** agrees in gender/number with the subject: lleno / llena / llenos / llenas.

**El café** is masculine — **el café**, **un café**. The accent on **é** is part of the spelling.
**Nos encontramos en el café** — **nos encontramos** is reflexive (encontrarse = to meet each other). The reflexive pronoun **nos** signals a mutual action.
**En el café** — use **en** for being at a location. Compare: **Vamos al café** (we're going to the café).

**El hotel** is masculine — **el hotel**, **un hotel**.
**Está en el centro** uses **estar** — location is always expressed with **estar**, never **ser**.
**El centro** = the city centre / downtown. Full form: **el centro de la ciudad**.
From Latin **hospes** (host/guest) — same family as **hospital**, **hostal**, **hospedaje**.
cards.phrase: El hotel está en el centro.

cards.grammarNote:
**El aeropuerto** is masculine. Etymology: **aero** (air, from Greek **aer**) + **puerto** (port/harbour) — literally *air port*, matching the English word.
**Puerto** alone = port/harbour: **el puerto de Barcelona**.
**Está lejos de aquí** — location uses **estar**. **Lejos de** = far from; **cerca de** = near.
cards.englishPhrase: The airport is far from here.
cards.phrase: El aeropuerto está lejos de aquí.

cards.grammarNote:
**La estación** is feminine (all **-ción** nouns are feminine: la nación, la canción, la estación).
**Cerca del hotel** — **del** = **de + el** (mandatory contraction). You can't write *de el hotel*.
**Está cerca** — location with **estar**; **cerca de** = near.
cards.englishPhrase: The station is near the hotel.
cards.phrase: La estación está cerca del hotel.

cards.grammarNote:
**La parada** (feminine) = the stop. **Parada de autobús** = bus stop; **parada de metro** = metro stop.
**Espera en la parada** — **Espera** is the informal (tú) imperative of **esperar**. Formal: **Espere**.
**En** here means *at* (being at a location). **Autobús** (Spain) = **bus** (Latin America); also **camión** (Mexico), **colectivo** (Argentina).
cards.phrase: Espera en la parada de autobús.

cards.grammarNote:
**El parque** is masculine — **el parque**, **un parque**.
**Juegan en el parque** — **jugar** (to play a game/sport) uses **en** for location. Note: **jugar** ≠ **tocar**: **jugar al fútbol** (play football) but **tocar la guitarra** (play the guitar).
**Los niños juegan** — stem-changing verb: **juego**, **juegas**, **juega**, **jugamos**, **jugáis**, **juegan** (u→ue except nosotros/vosotros).
cards.englishPhrase: The children play in the park.
cards.phrase: Los niños juegan en el parque.

cards.grammarNote:
**La farmacia** is feminine — **la farmacia**, **una farmacia**.
**¿Hay una farmacia cerca?** — **hay** (from **haber**) = there is / there are. It's invariable: **hay una farmacia**, **hay dos farmacias**.
**Cerca** = nearby (no **de** needed when no specific reference follows). **Cerca de aquí** = near here.

**La calle** is feminine (unusual since most **-e** nouns can go either way — just memorise this one).
**Está en esta calle** — location uses **estar**. **Esta** = this (feminine demonstrative, agrees with **calle**).
**Esta** (no accent) = this (adjective); **ésta** (old spelling with accent) = this one (pronoun — now the accent is optional).
cards.englishPhrase: The restaurant is on this street.
cards.phrase: El restaurante está en esta calle.

cards.grammarNote:
**El puente** is masculine.
**Cruzamos el puente** — past tense (preterite) of **cruzar** (nosotros form). The preterite ending **-amos** is the same for present and past with -ar verbs for nosotros — context clarifies tense.
**El puente** also colloquially means a long weekend (a 'bridge' between a holiday and the weekend).

**La esquina** is feminine — the corner of a street/building.
**Dobla a la derecha** — **a la derecha** (to the right), **a la izquierda** (to the left). These phrases always use **a + la** because **derecha** and **izquierda** are feminine nouns.
**Doblar** and **girar** both mean 'to turn' when giving directions — both are common.
cards.phrase: Dobla a la derecha en la esquina.

cards.grammarNote:
**El centro** is masculine. Full form: **el centro de la ciudad** (city centre).
**El museo está en el centro** — location uses **estar** + **en**.
**El museo** is also masculine. Many cultural buildings are masculine: **el museo**, **el teatro**, **el estadio**, **el cine**.
cards.phrase: El museo está en el centro.

cards.grammarNote:
**El barrio** is masculine — **el barrio**, **un barrio**.
**Vivo en un barrio tranquilo** — use **en** for residence location. **Tranquilo** (quiet/calm) is an adjective that agrees with the masculine noun: **barrio tranquilo** / **calle tranquila**.
In many cities, neighbourhoods have famous names: **el Barrio Gótico** (Barcelona), **el Barrio de La Boca** (Buenos Aires).
cards.englishPhrase: I live in a quiet neighbourhood.

cards.grammarNote:
**La playa** is feminine — **la playa**, **una playa**.
**La playa es hermosa** — use **ser** for a permanent or inherent quality (beauty of a place). Compare: **La playa está llena** (the beach is crowded — temporary state, usar **estar**).
**Hermosa** (beautiful) is the feminine form; **hermoso** for masculine.

**La montaña** is feminine — **la montaña**, **una montaña**.
**Es muy alta** uses **ser** — height/size is an inherent characteristic of a mountain.
**Alta** is the feminine form of **alto** (tall/high). Adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they describe.

**El museo** is masculine.
**Quiero visitar el museo** — **querer + infinitive** = to want to do something. **Quiero** is a stem-changing verb (e→ie): quiero, quieres, quiere, queremos, queréis, quieren.
**Visitar** (to visit a place) takes a direct object with no preposition: **visitar el museo**, **visitar la ciudad**.
cards.englishPhrase: I want to visit the museum.

cards.grammarNote:
**El cine** is masculine — short for **cinematógrafo**.
**Vamos al cine** — **al** = **a + el** (mandatory contraction). You can never write *a el cine*.
**Esta noche** = tonight. **Ir al cine** is the standard phrase for going to the movies — the same as 'going to the cinema' in British English.
cards.englishPhrase: We're going to the cinema tonight.

cards.grammarNote:
**El mapa** is masculine — despite ending in **-a** (which usually signals feminine). Other masculine **-a** nouns: **el problema**, **el programa**, **el tema**, **el día**. Many come from Greek.
**¿Tienes un mapa?** — informal question using **tú** form. Formal: **¿Tiene usted un mapa?**

**La dirección** is feminine (all **-ción** nouns are feminine).
**¿En qué dirección está?** — use **estar** for location. **En qué** = in which / what.
**Dirección** also means *address* (postal address) — context makes it clear: **¿Cuál es tu dirección?** (What's your address?)

**En** covers both *in* and *at* for location: **en la bolsa** (in the bag), **en la oficina** (at the office), **en el aeropuerto** (at the airport).
**Las llaves están en la bolsa** — location uses **estar**. **Las llaves** (the keys) is feminine plural.
Contrast **en** (location/state) with **a** (direction/destination): **Estoy en casa** vs **Voy a casa**.
cards.englishPhrase: The keys are in the bag.
cards.phrase: Las llaves están en la bolsa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Sobre** = on top of / above / about. **El libro está sobre la mesa** = The book is on the table.
**Encima de** is a near-synonym meaning *on top of*: **encima de la mesa** — slightly more emphatic about vertical position.
**En** can also mean *on* in some contexts: **en la mesa** (on the table) is equally natural and very common.
cards.englishPhrase: The book is on the table.
cards.phrase: El libro está sobre la mesa.

cards.grammarNote:
Spanish uses **en** for both *in* and *at* with locations: **Estoy en la oficina** = I'm at/in the office.
**Estoy** is from **estar** — always use **estar** (not **ser**) for location.
The key contrast: **en** (being somewhere) vs **a** (going somewhere): **Estoy en el banco** (I'm at the bank) vs **Voy al banco** (I'm going to the bank).

**Debajo de** = under/below. Always two words, always followed by **de**.
**Debajo de la mesa** — **de + la** stays as **de la** (no contraction needed; contractions only apply to **de + el**).
Compare position prepositions: **encima de** (on top of) · **debajo de** (under) · **al lado de** (next to) · **delante de** (in front of) · **detrás de** (behind).
cards.englishPhrase: The cat is under the table.
cards.phrase: El gato está debajo de la mesa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Al lado de** = next to / beside. Broken down: **al** (= **a + el**) + **lado** (side) + **de** (of).
**Al lado del café** — **del** = **de + el** (mandatory contraction). The phrase contains *two* contractions: **al** and **del**.
Other position prepositions follow the same **[prep] + de** pattern: **cerca de**, **lejos de**, **delante de**, **detrás de**, **encima de**, **debajo de**.
cards.englishPhrase: The bank is next to the cafe.
cards.phrase: El banco está al lado del café.

cards.grammarNote:
**Entre** = between (two things) or among (more than two). Unlike most position words, it does NOT need **de**: **entre la escuela y la biblioteca** (not *entre de*).
**El parque está entre...** — location uses **estar**.
**Y** = and. Before words starting with **i** or **hi**, **y** changes to **e**: **padre e hijo** (father and son).
cards.englishPhrase: The park is between the school and the library.
cards.phrase: El parque está entre la escuela y la biblioteca.

cards.grammarNote:
**En frente de** = in front of. Also written as **enfrente de** (one word). Both are correct.
**En frente del hotel** — **del** = **de + el** (mandatory contraction).
Compare: **delante de** (physically in front of, e.g., leading the way) vs **enfrente de** (facing/opposite, e.g., across the street).
cards.englishPhrase: The taxi is in front of the hotel.
cards.phrase: El taxi está en frente del hotel.

cards.grammarNote:
**Detrás de** = behind. Always followed by **de**.
**Detrás de la casa** — **de + la** = **de la** (no contraction; only **de + el** contracts to **del**).
Position preposition family: **delante de** (in front of) · **detrás de** (behind) · **encima de** (on top of) · **debajo de** (under) · **al lado de** (next to) · **enfrente de** (facing).
cards.englishPhrase: The garden is behind the house.
cards.phrase: El jardín está detrás de la casa.

cards.grammarNote:
**Cerca de** = near. **Cerca de aquí** = near here. When followed by a masculine noun: **cerca del banco** (del = de + el).
**¿Hay un restaurante cerca de aquí?** — **hay** (there is) introduces new/indefinite information. Compare: **¿Dónde está el restaurante?** (where is the [specific] restaurant — **está** for known/specific).
**Cerca** alone (no **de**) = nearby: **¿Hay una farmacia cerca?**
cards.englishPhrase: Is there a restaurant near here?

cards.grammarNote:
**Lejos de** = far from. Opposite of **cerca de** (near).
**¿Está lejos el aeropuerto?** — inverted word order for questions is natural in Spanish (subject after verb). **El aeropuerto** = **el** + masculine noun.
**El aeropuerto** — etymology: **aero** (air) + **puerto** (port). The same compound in English: *air + port*.

Three words for 'here': **aquí** (here, right at this spot — most common), **acá** (here, more general — common in Latin America), **aca** (informal variant).
**Ven aquí** — **Ven** is the irregular informal imperative of **venir**. Formal: **Venga aquí**.
**Por favor** = please (literally 'by/for favour'). Always a polite addition when making requests.

Three words for 'there': **aquí** (here) · **allí** (there, at a specific spot) · **allá** (over there, more vague/distant).
**El taxi está allí** — location uses **estar**.
**Allí mismo** = right there (very precise); **allá lejos** = way over there (distant). The distinction between **allí** and **allá** mirrors **aquí** vs **acá**.

**A la izquierda** = to the left. The full direction phrase always uses **a + la** because **izquierda** is feminine.
**Gira a la izquierda** (turn left) — one of the three essential direction commands alongside **a la derecha** (right) and **todo recto** (straight ahead).
Remember: **izquierda** and **derecha** are nouns (feminine), not adjectives. That's why they take an article: **a la izquierda**, not *a izquierda*.

**A la derecha** = to the right. Like **izquierda**, **derecha** is a feminine noun and always takes **a + la**.
**Gira a la derecha** (turn right) · **Gira a la izquierda** (turn left) · **Ve todo recto** (go straight).
**Derecho/a** (adjective) = straight: **todo recto** or **todo derecho**. Don't confuse **derecha** (direction: right) with **derecho** (straight ahead or the noun 'right/law').

**Todo recto** = straight ahead (literally 'all straight'). Both **todo recto** and **todo derecho** are used — **todo recto** is slightly more common in directions.
**Ve todo recto** — **Ve** is the irregular informal imperative of **ir** (to go). Formal: **Vaya todo recto**.
This completes the trio of essential direction phrases: **a la derecha** · **a la izquierda** · **todo recto**.

**Al norte** = to the north. The contraction **al** = **a + el** is used even with compass directions since they are treated as masculine nouns.
All four cardinal directions are masculine: **el norte**, **el sur**, **el este**, **el oeste**.
Compass direction phrases: **al norte** (to/in the north), **al sur** (south), **al este** (east), **al oeste** (west).
cards.englishPhrase: The city is to the north.

cards.grammarNote:
**Al sur** = to the south. **Al** = **a + el** (mandatory contraction — **sur** is masculine).
**La playa está al sur** — location with **estar**. The beach is located (permanently, for this context) to the south.
Cardinal directions: **norte** · **sur** · **este** · **oeste** — all masculine, all use **al** when saying 'to the [direction]'.
cards.englishPhrase: The beach is to the south.

cards.grammarNote:
**El este** = the east (masculine). **Por el este** = through/via the east — **por** indicates movement through a direction.
**Sale por el este** — **salir por** = to come out through. The sun 'comes out' (**sale**) through the east.
Beware of homonyms: **este** (east, noun, no accent) · **este** (this, demonstrative adjective, no accent) · **éste** (this one, demonstrative pronoun — accent optional in modern Spanish).
cards.englishPhrase: The sun rises in the east.
cards.phrase: El sol sale por el este.

cards.grammarNote:
**El oeste** = the west (masculine). **En el oeste** = in the west.
**Se pone** — **ponerse** (to set, for the sun) is reflexive. The reflexive **se** signals an automatic/natural process. **El sol se pone** (the sun sets) · **el sol sale** (the sun rises).
**Poner** also means 'to put/place': context distinguishes. Reflexive **ponerse** = to put on (clothing) or to set (sun).
cards.englishPhrase: The sun sets in the west.
cards.phrase: El sol se pone en el oeste.

cards.grammarNote:
**Cerca** (no **de**) = nearby (standalone adverb, no specific reference).
**Cerca de** + noun = near [something]: **cerca de aquí** (near here), **cerca del banco** (near the bank — **del** = de + el).
**¿Hay una farmacia cerca?** — **hay** (there is/are) introduces indefinite existence. If you already know a specific pharmacy: **¿Dónde está la farmacia?** (Where is the pharmacy?).

**Ir** is highly irregular. Present tense: **voy**, **vas**, **va**, **vamos**, **vais**, **van**.
**Ir a + place** = to go to a place: **voy al supermercado**, **voy a casa**, **voy a la playa**.
**Ir a + infinitive** also expresses future: **voy a comer** (I'm going to eat), **vamos a salir** (we're going to leave).
**Al** = **a + el** (mandatory contraction) whenever the destination has a masculine article.

**Venir** is irregular. Present tense: **vengo**, **vienes**, **viene**, **venimos**, **venís**, **vienen**.
**Ven a mi casa** — **Ven** is the informal (tú) imperative.
**Venir a + place** = to come to a place. Contrast: **ir** (to go, away from speaker) vs **venir** (to come, towards speaker) — same speaker-relative logic as English.

**Me encanta viajar** — **encantar** works like **gustar**: the subject is the thing loved (**viajar**), not the person. **Me** = indirect object (to me). Literally: 'travelling enchants me'.
Single thing/verb: **me encanta** · Multiple things: **me encantan los viajes**.
**Viajar** is a regular **-ar** verb: viajo, viajas, viaja, viajamos, viajáis, viajan.

**Camino al trabajo** — **al** = **a + el** (mandatory contraction before masculine noun **trabajo**).
**Caminar** is a regular **-ar** verb. Also common: **andar** (to walk/go on foot) — more colloquial in Spain.
**Todos los días** = every day (literally 'all the days'). Compare: **cada día** (each day) — both are common and interchangeable.
cards.englishPhrase: I walk to work every day.
cards.phrase: Camino al trabajo todos los días.

cards.grammarNote:
**Manejar** = to drive (Latin America). In Spain: **conducir** (irregular: conduzco, conduces…).
**Maneja a la oficina** — **a la** because **oficina** is feminine. Compare masculine: **al trabajo** (to work), **al banco** (to the bank).
**Ella** (she) is optional — Spanish drops subject pronouns since verb endings identify the subject.

**Gira a la izquierda** — the three core direction commands:
**Gira a la derecha** (turn right) · **Gira a la izquierda** (turn left) · **Ve todo recto** (go straight ahead).
**Gira** is the informal (tú) imperative of **girar**. Formal (usted): **Gire a la izquierda**.
Alternative: **doblar** — **dobla a la derecha** is equally natural.
cards.phrase: Gira a la izquierda en la esquina.

cards.grammarNote:
**Cruza la calle** — **Cruza** is the informal (tú) imperative of **cruzar**. Formal: **Cruce la calle**.
**Con cuidado** = carefully (literally 'with care'). **Cuidado** is also used as a standalone warning: **¡Cuidado!** = Watch out!
**Cruzar** is a regular **-ar** verb: cruzo, cruzas, cruza… Note spelling change in preterite (yo): **crucé** (not *cruzé*).

**Sigue esta calle** — **Sigue** is the informal (tú) imperative of **seguir**. Formal: **Siga esta calle**.
**Seguir** is irregular: **sigo**, sigues, sigue, seguimos, seguís, siguen (yo form has irregular **g**).
**Seguir + gerund** = to keep doing something: **sigue recto** (keep going straight), **sigue caminando** (keep walking).

**Entra por la puerta** — **entrar por** = to enter through. The preposition is **por** (through/by way of), not **en**.
**Entrar en** is also used (especially in Spain): **entra en el edificio** (enter the building). Latin American Spanish often omits **en**: **entra al edificio**.
**La puerta principal** — **principal** = main. Adjectives follow the noun in Spanish.

**Salir** is irregular in yo: **salgo** (I leave/go out). Other forms are regular: sales, sale, salimos, salís, salen.
**Salgo del trabajo** — **del** = **de + el** (mandatory contraction). You can never write *de el trabajo*.
**A las cinco** = at five (o'clock). Time expressions use **a las** (feminine plural) because **hora** (hour) is feminine: **a la una**, **a las dos**, **a las cinco**.
cards.phrase: Salgo del trabajo a las cinco.

cards.grammarNote:
**Llegar** = to arrive. Regular **-ar** verb (with a spelling change in preterite yo: **llegué**).
**Llegamos mañana** — **llegamos** is both present (we arrive) and preterite (we arrived) for nosotros; **mañana** (tomorrow) here confirms it's present/future.
**Llegar a** + place = to arrive at: **llegamos a Madrid**, **llegamos al hotel** (**al** = a + el).

**Quiero visitar el museo** — **querer + infinitive** expresses wanting to do something.
**Visitar** is a regular **-ar** verb: visito, visitas, visita, visitamos, visitáis, visitan.
**Visitar** takes a direct object with no preposition: **visitar el museo**, **visitar a un amigo** (personal 'a' before a person — **a** before a specific human direct object is mandatory in Spanish).
cards.englishPhrase: I want to visit the museum.

cards.grammarNote:
**Vivir** = to live. Regular **-ir** verb: **vivo**, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven.
**Vivo cerca del centro** — **del** = **de + el** (mandatory contraction). **Cerca de** = near.
**Vivir en** = to live in/at a place. **Vivo en Madrid**, **vivo en un apartamento**, **vivo cerca del centro**.
cards.englishPhrase: I live near the city centre.

cards.grammarNote:
**Quedarse** = to stay/remain (reflexive). The phrase uses **hospedarse** instead — a more specific word meaning to lodge/stay as a guest.
**Nos hospedamos** — reflexive verb with **nos** (we). **Hospedarse** comes from Latin **hospes** (host/guest) — same root as **hospital**, **hotel**, **hostal**.
**Quedarse en** = to stay at: **me quedo en el hotel** (I'm staying at the hotel).

**Te espero** = I'll wait for you. **Esperar a alguien** = to wait for someone — the 'for' is built into the verb; no preposition needed before the person.
**Te** = you (indirect object pronoun, informal). Formal: **Le espero**.
**Esperar** also means *to hope*: **espero que llegues pronto** (I hope you arrive soon). Context distinguishes.

**Quedamos en el parque** uses **quedar** (to arrange to meet) — very natural in Spain for planned meetings.
**Quedar en** = to meet at (a place). Alternative: **encontrarse en**: **nos encontramos en el parque**.
**Quedar** has many meanings: to remain (**queda poco tiempo** = little time remains), to fit (**te queda bien** = it suits you), to arrange to meet (**quedamos a las tres** = let's meet at three).

**Perderse** is reflexive — the pronoun changes with the subject:
**me pierdo** · **te pierdes** · **se pierde**
Many movement/location verbs are reflexive: **quedarse** (to stay), **hospedarse** (to lodge), **dirigirse** (to head)
**¡No te pierdas!** = Don't get lost!

**No encuentro el hotel** — **encontrar** is a stem-changing verb (o→ue): **encuentro**, encuentras, encuentra, encontramos, encontráis, encuentran.
**No encuentro** = I can't find / I don't find. Spanish present tense covers the English 'can't find' in this context.
Contrast: **encontrar** (to find something) vs **encontrarse** (reflexive: to be located, or to meet someone).

**Busco la farmacia** — **buscar** means 'to look for'. The 'for' is already inside the verb — never add **por** or **para**: say **busco el hotel**, not *busco por el hotel*.
**Buscar** is a regular **-ar** verb (with spelling change in preterite yo: **busqué**).
**La farmacia** — feminine noun. Pharmacies in Spanish-speaking countries are marked by a green cross.

**Para en la esquina** — **Para** is the informal (tú) imperative of **parar** (to stop). Formal: **Pare en la esquina**.
**Parar** (transitive) = to stop something; **pararse** (reflexive) = to stop oneself/come to a stop.
Also common: **detenerse** = to stop (slightly more formal): **detente aquí** (stop here).

**Aparcar** (Spain) / **estacionar** (Latin America) = to park a vehicle. Both are correct.
**¿Dónde puedo estacionar?** — **poder + infinitive** = to be able to / can. **Puedo** is the yo form (stem-changing: o→ue): **puedo**, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden.
**Dónde** = where (with accent in questions). Without accent: **donde** = where (in relative clauses).

**El mercado está muy concurrido** — use **estar** (not **ser**) because crowdedness is a temporary state.
**Concurrido** agrees with the subject: **mercado concurrido** (m.) · **calle concurrida** (f.) · **lugares concurridos** (m.pl.) · **calles concurridas** (f.pl.).
Alternatives: **lleno** (full) · **animado** (lively) · **transitado** (busy with traffic).

**Prefiero un barrio tranquilo** — **tranquilo** = quiet/calm. It follows the noun it modifies (adjectives usually follow in Spanish).
**Tranquilo** agrees with the noun: **barrio tranquilo** (m.) · **calle tranquila** (f.) · **lugares tranquilos** (m.pl.).
**Prefiero** = I prefer (stem-changing verb e→ie): prefiero, prefieres, prefiere, preferimos, preferís, prefieren.

**Estoy perdido** — use **estar** (not **ser**) because being lost is a temporary state.
**Perdido** (m.) / **perdida** (f.) — the adjective agrees with the subject: **estoy perdido** (male speaker) · **estoy perdida** (female speaker).
Related: **perderse** (to get lost — reflexive): **me perdí** (I got lost) · **¡No te pierdas!** (Don't get lost!)

Use **ser** for professions — and omit the article:
**Soy médico** ✓ (not *Soy un médico*) · **Es enfermera** · **Es ingeniero**
The article returns only when the noun is modified: **Soy un buen médico**

Gender forms: **el enfermero** (male nurse) / **la enfermera** (female nurse).
From Latin **infirmus** (sick/weak) — compare English "infirmary".
Use **ser** for the profession without an article: **Es enfermera** (She is a nurse).

Gender forms: **el ingeniero** / **la ingeniera**.
From Latin **ingenium** (cleverness, talent, natural ability) — the same root as English "engine" and "ingenious".
Use **ser** without an article: **Mi hermano es ingeniero** (My brother is an engineer).

Gender forms: **el programador** / **la programadora**.
**Trabajo como programador** uses **como** (as/like) — an alternative to **ser**: **soy programador** and **trabajo como programador** both work.
**Trabajar como** is especially natural when describing a current role rather than a permanent identity.

Gender forms: **el cocinero** / **la cocinera**.
Note the double meaning of **cocina**: it means both "kitchen" (the room) and "cooking/cuisine" (the activity).
**La cocina italiana** = Italian cuisine · **trabajar en la cocina** = to work in the kitchen.
A professional chef is often called **el/la chef** (borrowed from French).
cards.englishPhrase: The cook works in the kitchen.
cards.phrase: El cocinero trabaja en la cocina.

cards.grammarNote:
Gender forms: **el camarero** / **la camarera** (Spain).
In Latin America you'll often hear **el mesero / la mesera** instead.
**Trajo** is the preterite (past tense) of **traer** (to bring) — an irregular verb: traje, trajiste, trajo, trajimos, trajeron.
Note the accent on **menú** — required because the stress falls on the final syllable.

**Gerente** is a shared-gender noun: **el gerente** / **la gerente** (the ending doesn't change).
This is common with nouns ending in **-ente** or **-ante**: **el/la estudiante**, **el/la presidente**, **el/la asistente**.
Another word for manager: **el/la director(a)** (director), **el/la jefe/jefa** (boss/chief).

**Estudiante** is a shared-gender noun: **el estudiante** / **la estudiante** — the word itself doesn't change.
This is typical of nouns ending in **-nte**: **el/la asistente**, **el/la presidente**, **el/la gerente**.
Use **ser** without an article for professions/roles: **Soy estudiante** (I am a student) — not *Soy un estudiante*.

Gender forms: **el arquitecto** / **la arquitecta**.
From Greek **arkhitekton** (master builder): **arkhi-** (chief) + **tekton** (builder) — same root as English "architect".
Use **ser** without an article: **Él es arquitecto** (He is an architect).
Related word: **la arquitectura** (architecture).

Gender forms: **el abogado** / **la abogada**.
From Latin **advocatus** (one called to help) — same root as English "advocate".
Notice the example: **Mi hermana es abogada** — the profession agrees in gender with the subject (**hermana** → **abogada**).
Related: **el derecho** (law/right), **el bufete** (law firm).

**El salario** = salary — from Latin **salarium** (allowance to buy salt, **sal**), hence the English word "salary".
Also common: **el sueldo** (wage/pay — more colloquial than **salario**).
**¿Cuál es el salario?** — use **cuál** (which/what) before **es** when asking about identity/value (not **qué**).
**Cuál vs. qué**: **¿Cuál es tu nombre?** (What is your name? — selection from a set) vs. **¿Qué es el amor?** (What is love? — definition).

**El horario** = schedule/timetable — from **hora** (hour) + **-ario** (a suffix for things related to something).
**Flexible** is an invariable adjective: **mi horario es flexible** / **mis horarios son flexibles** — same form for masculine/feminine.
**Mi horario es flexible** uses **ser** because schedule type is an inherent characteristic.
Related: **el turno** (shift/turn), **jornada completa** (full-time), **media jornada** (part-time), **hora punta** (rush hour).

**Vacaciones** is almost always used in the plural in Spanish — even for a single trip: **voy de vacaciones** (not *voy de vacación*).
**Ir de vacaciones** = to go on vacation — note **de**, not *en*: **voy de vacaciones** (I'm going on vacation).
**La semana próxima** = next week — **próximo** (next) follows the noun for time: **el mes próximo**, **el año próximo**. Alternatively, **próxima semana** or **la semana que viene** (the week that comes) are also common.
cards.englishPhrase: I'm going on vacation next week.
cards.phrase: Voy de vacaciones la semana próxima.

cards.grammarNote:
**El descanso** = break/rest — from **descansar** (to rest).
**Tomar un descanso** = to take a break — **tomar** (literally "to take/drink") is used in many fixed expressions: **tomar un café** (to have a coffee), **tomar asiento** (to take a seat), **tomar una decisión** (to make a decision).
**Tomemos** is the nosotros imperative (let's take): formed from the subjunctive **tomemos**.
Related: **descansar** (to rest), **el recreo** (school recess/break), **la pausa** (pause).

**La oficina** = office (the room/workplace).
From Latin **officina** (workshop, place of work) — same root as English "office".
**Trabajo en una oficina** — **en** for location (in/at): **en casa** (at home), **en el hospital** (at the hospital).
Related: **el despacho** (personal office/study — Spain), **la empresa** (company/firm), **el edificio de oficinas** (office building).

**El compañero / la compañera** = companion/colleague — from Latin **companio** (one who shares bread: **com-** together + **panis** bread).
**Compañero de trabajo** = work colleague — **de** specifies the context: **compañero de clase** (classmate), **compañero de piso** (roommate).
**Son simpáticos** uses **ser** for personality: **simpático/a** = friendly/pleasant (a permanent trait).
Note the plural adjective agreement: **compañeros** (m.pl.) → **simpáticos** (m.pl.).
cards.phrase: Mis compañeros de trabajo son simpáticos.

cards.grammarNote:
**El cliente / la cliente** — shared-gender noun (the article changes, the word stays the same).
Also acceptable: **la clienta** (feminine form, less common but used in Spain).
**El cliente está contento** — **estar** for current emotional state (not **ser**): **está contento** = is happy right now.
Compare: **ser contento** is not used; for happiness as a state, always use **estar**.
Related: **la clientela** (clientele/customer base), **atender a un cliente** (to serve a customer).

**El equipo** = team (work context) or equipment (sports/technical context) — context clarifies.
**Trabajo en un equipo genial** — **en** for membership: **trabajar en un equipo** (to work on a team), **jugar en un equipo** (to play on a team).
**Genial** = great/awesome (colloquial) — literally "genial/genius-like". An invariable adjective: **un equipo genial** / **una idea genial**.
Note: in team sports, Spanish treats the team as a collective singular: **el equipo juega** (the team plays).
cards.englishPhrase: I work in a great team.

cards.grammarNote:
**El proyecto** = project — from Latin **projectum** (thrown forward): **pro-** (forward) + **jacere** (to throw). Same root as English "project".
**El proyecto está casi terminado** — **estar** + past participle describes a resulting state: **está terminado** (is finished/completed), **está abierto** (is open), **está cerrado** (is closed).
**Terminado** is the past participle of **terminar**, used here as an adjective agreeing with **proyecto** (masculine).
**Casi** = almost/nearly — an adverb, doesn't change form.

**La reunión** = meeting — from **reunir** (to gather/unite): **re-** (again) + **unir** (to unite).
**Tenemos una reunión a las diez** — **tener** is used for scheduled events.
**A las diez** = at ten (o'clock) — plural **las** because it's more than one: **a la una** (at one), **a las dos** (at two), **a las diez** (at ten).
Related: **reunirse** (reflexive: to meet/gather), **convocar una reunión** (to call a meeting).
cards.englishPhrase: We have a meeting at ten.
cards.phrase: Tenemos una reunión a las diez.

cards.grammarNote:
**El tiempo libre** = free time — **libre** (free/unoccupied) as opposed to **ocupado** (busy).
**¿Qué haces en tu tiempo libre?** — **haces** is the tú form of **hacer**: **hago, haces, hace, hacemos...**
