Note: **¿Qué haces?** (What do you do?) vs. **¿Qué estás haciendo?** (What are you doing right now?).
**Tiempo** has two meanings: **time** (el tiempo libre) and **weather** (¿Qué tiempo hace? — What's the weather like?). Context always clarifies.
cards.englishPhrase: What do you do in your free time?

cards.grammarNote:
**Trabajar** is a regular -ar verb: **trabajo, trabajas, trabaja, trabajamos, trabajáis, trabajan**.
Preposition choices: **trabajar en** + place (**trabajo en un hospital** — I work in a hospital), **trabajar como** + profession (**trabajo como enfermera** — I work as a nurse), **trabajar de** + profession (also common: **trabajo de cocinero**).
**Dedicarse a** = to devote oneself to / to work as: **Se dedica a la medicina** (She devotes herself to medicine).

**Me gusta leer** — with **gustar**, use the infinitive for activities: **Me gusta leer, nadar, cocinar**.
For multiple activities, **gustan** is NOT used — keep **gusta** with a list of infinitives: **Me gusta leer y cocinar**.
**Leer** has a spelling change in the gerund: **leyendo** (not *leiendo*) — the unstressed **i** between vowels becomes **y**.
Same pattern: **creer → creyendo**, **caer → cayendo**.

**A ella le gusta escribir** — the **a + pronoun** construction clarifies who likes something, since **le** alone is ambiguous (could be he/she/you formal).
**Escribir** vs. **escribir a mano** (to write by hand) vs. **teclear** (to type).
Related nouns: **la escritura** (writing/script), **el escritor / la escritora** (writer), **el cuento** (short story).
cards.phrase: A ella le gusta escribir cuentos.

cards.grammarNote:
**A él le encanta pintar** — **encantar** is a stronger form of **gustar** (to love, to adore).
Both **gustar** and **encantar** are "reverse" verbs: the thing enjoyed is the grammatical subject.
**Pintar** (to paint) → **el pintor / la pintora** (painter), **la pintura** (painting/paint), **el cuadro** (painting/picture).
Note: **pintar** covers both painting a wall and creating art — context distinguishes them.

**Dibujar** = to draw (art/sketching). Not to be confused with **dibujos animados** (cartoons/animated drawings).
**Me gusta dibujar** — infinitive after **gustar** for activities.
Related nouns: **el dibujo** (drawing/sketch), **el dibujante / la dibujante** (illustrator/draughtsperson).
Compare: **pintar** (to paint with color), **dibujar** (to draw with lines/pencil).

**Escuchar música** = to listen to music — **escuchar** already means "to listen to", so no preposition is needed (unlike English).
Don't confuse **escuchar** (to listen to, attentively) with **oír** (to hear, passively): **Oigo música** (I hear music in the background) vs. **Escucho música** (I'm actively listening to music).
**Todos los días** = every day — note **todos** (all, masculine plural) agrees with **días**.
cards.englishPhrase: I listen to music every day.

cards.grammarNote:
**Cantar** = to sing. The person who sings is **el cantante / la cantante** (singer) — a shared-gender noun ending in **-ante**.
**A ella le encanta cantar** — **encantar** (to love/adore) works just like **gustar** but is stronger.
Related: **la canción** (song), **el coro** (choir/chorus), **afinar** (to tune/to sing in tune).

**Tocar** is the correct verb for playing an instrument — never **jugar**.
**Toco la guitarra** · **toca el piano** · **tocamos el violín**
Use **jugar** for sports and games: **jugar al fútbol**, **jugar ajedrez**.
Instruments take the definite article: **toco la guitarra** (not *toco guitarra*).
Related: **el instrumento** (instrument), **la guitarra acústica / eléctrica** (acoustic / electric guitar).

**Nos encanta bailar** — **nos** is the indirect object pronoun for "us".
**Encantar** conjugates to agree with the grammatical subject (what is loved), not the person: **nos encanta** (one thing) vs. **nos encantan** (multiple things).
Related: **el baile** (dance/dancing), **la bailarina / el bailarín** (ballet dancer), **el salón de baile** (ballroom).
**Bailar** is also used in expressions: **bailar salsa/tango/flamenco**.

**Cocinar** (to cook) vs. **cocina** (kitchen / cuisine) — same root, different form.
**Me gusta cocinar** — infinitive after **gustar** for activities.
For professional cooking, use **el cocinero / la cocinera** (cook) or **el/la chef**.
**Practicar** is used for hobbies/sports in general, but **cocinar** is the direct verb: say **me gusta cocinar**, not *practico la cocina* (unnatural).

**Hacer senderismo** = to go hiking — many outdoor activities in Spanish use **hacer**: **hacer senderismo**, **hacer yoga**, **hacer ejercicio**, **hacer surf**.
Alternatively: **ir de senderismo** (to go hiking).
**Senderismo** comes from **sendero** (path/trail).
Related: **la montaña** (mountain), **el monte** (hill/mountain/wilderness), **la ruta** (route/trail).
cards.englishPhrase: I like hiking in the mountains.
cards.phrase: Me gusta hacer senderismo en la montaña.

cards.grammarNote:
**Correr** = to run (a regular -er verb).
**Corro** (I run), **corres**, **corre**, **corremos**, **corréis**, **corren**.
**Todas las mañanas** = every morning — **todas** (all, feminine plural) agrees with **mañanas**.
Compare: **correr** (to run in general) vs. **trotar** (to jog at a light pace) vs. **hacer running** (to go for a run, borrowed term).

**Nadar** = to swim (a regular -ar verb).
**Me gusta nadar** — infinitive after **gustar** for activities.
For "to go swimming" use **ir a nadar** or **ir a la piscina** (to go to the pool).
Related: **la piscina** (pool), **el mar** (sea), **la playa** (beach), **el nadador / la nadadora** (swimmer).
**Practicar la natación** (to practice swimming) is also used in more formal contexts.

**Andar en bicicleta** = to ride a bike — literally "to walk/go by bicycle".
Also common: **montar en bicicleta** (especially in Spain) or **ir en bici** (informal).
**Andar** here means "to go/travel" rather than "to walk on foot".
**Los fines de semana** = on weekends — **el fin de semana** (the weekend), plural **los fines de semana**.
cards.phrase: Ando en bicicleta los fines de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Me encanta viajar** — **encantar** + infinitive = to love doing something.
**Viajar** is a regular -ar verb: **viajo, viajas, viaja, viajamos, viajáis, viajan**.
Related: **el viaje** (trip/journey), **el viajero / la viajera** (traveler), **viajar al extranjero** (to travel abroad).
**Ir de viaje** (to go on a trip) is a common alternative expression.

Stem-changing verb: **jugar** (u→ue): **juego, juegas, juega, jugamos, jugáis, juegan**.
With video games, **jugar** is used directly or with **a**: **juega videojuegos** or **juega a los videojuegos**.
Compare with sports: **jugar al fútbol** (requires **al**) — with videojuegos, the **a** is often dropped in informal speech.
**Por la noche** = at night/in the evening — compare: **por la mañana** (in the morning), **por la tarde** (in the afternoon).
cards.englishPhrase: He plays video games at night.
cards.phrase: Él juega videojuegos por la noche.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ver** = to watch/see (an irregular yo form: **veo**): **veo, ves, ve, vemos, veis, ven**.
**Me gusta ver películas** — infinitive after **gustar**.
Distinction: **ver la tele/televisión** (to watch TV), **ver una película** (to watch a movie), **ver una serie** (to watch a series/show).
**Películas** (movies) from **película** — originally "film strip" (related to **piel**, skin/film).

**Escuchar** = to listen to — the "to" is built in, no extra preposition needed.
**A ella le gusta escuchar música** — the **a ella** clarifies who likes it, because **le** alone is ambiguous.
Distinction: **escuchar** (active, attentive listening) vs. **oír** (passive hearing).
Related: **el oyente** (listener), **la canción** (song), **el álbum** (album).
cards.phrase: A ella le gusta escuchar música.

cards.grammarNote:
**Hacer ejercicio** = to exercise — **hacer** is the go-to verb for physical activities.
**Voy al gimnasio** — **al** is the mandatory contraction of **a + el**: never *a el gimnasio*.
**Para + infinitive** expresses purpose: **voy al gimnasio para hacer ejercicio** (I go to the gym in order to exercise).
Related: **el gimnasio** (gym), **entrenarse** (to train/work out), **el entrenador / la entrenadora** (trainer).
cards.englishPhrase: I go to the gym for exercise.
cards.phrase: Voy al gimnasio para hacer ejercicio.

cards.grammarNote:
**Al aire libre** = outdoors / in the open air — a fixed expression: **al** (a + el) + **aire** (air) + **libre** (free/open).
**Al** is the mandatory contraction of **a + el**: **al parque**, **al trabajo**, **al aire libre**.
**Trabajar al aire libre** — many professions involve outdoor work: **jardinero, agricultor, guía turístico, bombero**.
Related: **afuera** (outside), **en el exterior** (on the outside/outdoors — more formal).

**Creativo** is a quality adjective that changes for gender and number: **creativo** (m.sg.) / **creativa** (f.sg.) / **creativos** (m.pl.) / **creativas** (f.pl.).
Note the example: **Ella es muy creativa** — the adjective agrees with **ella** (feminine), so **creativa**.
Use **ser** for permanent character traits: **es creativa** (she is creative by nature).
Related: **la creatividad** (creativity), **crear** (to create), **la creación** (creation).

**Interesante** is an invariable adjective — it does NOT change for gender: **un trabajo interesante** / **una idea interesante** (same form).
Adjectives ending in **-e** or consonants are typically invariable for gender (they still change for number: **interesantes**).
Use **ser** for inherent qualities: **Mi trabajo es interesante** (permanent characteristic).
Related: **interesar** (to interest) — works like **gustar**: **Me interesa la música** (Music interests me).

**Aburrido** changes for gender and number: **aburrido** (m.sg.) / **aburrida** (f.sg.) / **aburridos / aburridas** (plural).
Note: **La reunión fue aburrida** — the adjective agrees with **la reunión** (feminine).
**Fue** is the preterite of both **ser** and **ir** — they share the same preterite forms: **fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron**. Context clarifies meaning.
**Ser vs. estar with aburrido**: **ser aburrido** = to be a boring (person/thing by nature); **estar aburrido** = to feel bored (current state).

**Ganar** = to earn / to win / to gain (a regular -ar verb).
Context determines meaning: **ganar dinero** (to earn money), **ganar un partido** (to win a game), **ganar experiencia** (to gain experience).
**Buen** vs. **bueno**: the adjective **bueno** shortens to **buen** before a masculine singular noun: **buen salario**, **buen trabajo**, **buen hombre**.
**Salario** comes from Latin **salarium** — the allowance given to Roman soldiers to buy salt (**sal**).

**Jubilarse** is a reflexive verb — the reflexive pronoun changes with each subject: **me jubilo, te jubilas, se jubila, nos jubilamos...**
**Se jubiló** = she retired — preterite (past) tense, with the accent on the final syllable marking the preterite.
**El año pasado** = last year — **pasado** (past/last) follows the noun: **la semana pasada**, **el mes pasado**.
From **júbilo** (joy) — compare English "jubilee".
cards.phrase: Ella se jubiló el año pasado.

cards.grammarNote:
**Tener** = to have (an irregular -er verb): **tengo, tienes, tiene, tenemos, tenéis, tienen**.
Note the irregular yo form: **tengo** (not *teno*).
**Buen** shortens before masculine singular nouns: **buen trabajo**, **buen salario** (but **buena idea** with feminine nouns).
**Tener** vs. **haber**: **tener** = to have/possess; **hay** (from haber) = there is/there are.

**Estar desempleado** — use **estar** (not **ser**) for states that can change: unemployment is temporary.
Compare: **Soy médico** (I am a doctor — identity) vs. **Estoy desempleado** (I am unemployed — current state).
**Desempleado** = unemployed — from **des-** (un-) + **empleado** (employed, from **emplear**, to employ).
Alternatives: **estar en paro** (Spain, colloquial), **estar sin trabajo** (to be without work).

**Estudiar** = to study (a regular -ar verb): **estudio, estudias, estudia, estudiamos, estudiáis, estudian**.
**Todos los días** = every day — **todos** (all, masculine plural) agrees with **días** (days).
Compare **estudiar** (to study a subject) vs. **aprender** (to learn/acquire knowledge): **Estudio medicina** (I study medicine) vs. **Aprendo español** (I'm learning Spanish).

**Aprender** = to learn (a regular -er verb): **aprendo, aprendes, aprende, aprendemos, aprendéis, aprenden**.
**Estoy aprendiendo** = I am learning — present progressive: **estar** + gerund (**aprendiendo**).
In Spanish, the simple present often replaces the progressive for ongoing situations: **aprendo español** is equally natural.
Related: **el aprendizaje** (learning/apprenticeship), **aprender de memoria** (to memorize/learn by heart).

**Practicar** = to practice (a sport, hobby, or skill) — use this for non-game activities.
Don't use **jugar** for non-competitive activities: say **practico yoga**, **practico natación**, **practico senderismo**.
For sports framed as competition or play, **jugar** is also correct: **juego al tenis** (I play tennis) or **practico el tenis**.
**Practico** (I practice) — note the spelling change: **c → qu** before **e/i**: **practiqué** (I practiced, preterite).

**Enseñar** = to teach / to show (a regular -ar verb).
Note that **enseñar** means both "to teach" and "to show": **Me enseña la foto** (She shows me the photo) vs. **Enseña español** (She teaches Spanish).
The person who teaches: **el profesor / la profesora** (teacher/professor) — gender forms differ.
Related: **la enseñanza** (teaching/education), **el colegio** (school), **dar clases** (to give classes/teach).

**Construir** belongs to a group of -uir verbs that insert a **y** before vowel endings: **construyo, construyes, construye, construimos, construís, construyen**.
The gerund: **construyendo** (building) — the **y** appears there too.
**Están construyendo** = they are building — present progressive.
Related: **la construcción** (construction), **el constructor / la constructora** (builder), **el edificio** (building).
cards.englishPhrase: They are building a new school.

cards.grammarNote:
**Arreglar** = to fix / to arrange / to tidy (a regular -ar verb).
Context determines the meaning: **arreglar el coche** (to fix the car), **arreglar la habitación** (to tidy the room), **arreglarse** (to get ready/dressed up — reflexive).
**¿Puedes arreglar esto?** — **poder** (can/to be able to) is a stem-changing verb (o→ue): **puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden**.
**Esto** = this (neuter demonstrative, used when the noun is unspecified).

**Hacer** = to make / to do — one of the most versatile and irregular verbs in Spanish.
Irregular yo form: **hago** (not *haco*).
Full present: **hago, haces, hace, hacemos, hacéis, hacen**.
**Hacer** is used for many activities: **hacer ejercicio** (to exercise), **hacer yoga**, **hacer senderismo**, **hacer la tarea** (to do homework), **hacer una llamada** (to make a call).
**Hago café** — note no article needed: **hacer café**, **hacer ejercicio** (activity as a mass/abstract noun).

**Diseñar** = to design (a regular -ar verb).
The person who designs: **el diseñador / la diseñadora** (designer).
**Páginas web** = websites — literally "web pages". Also: **sitios web** (websites) or just **webs** (colloquial).
Related fields: **el diseño gráfico** (graphic design), **el diseño web** (web design), **el diseño industrial** (industrial design).
Compare with **dibujar** (to draw): **diseñar** implies intentional planning/creation for a purpose.

**Vender** = to sell (a regular -er verb): **vendo, vendes, vende, vendemos, vendéis, venden**.
The person who sells: **el vendedor / la vendedora** (salesperson/seller).
Related: **la venta** (sale), **en venta** (for sale), **comprar** (to buy — the opposite).
Note: **coches** (cars) is the Spain variant; in Latin America you'll hear **carros** or **autos** instead.

**Comprar** = to buy (a regular -ar verb): **compro, compras, compra, compramos, compráis, compran**.
**Necesito comprar** — **necesitar + infinitive** = to need to do something: **necesito estudiar** (I need to study).
**Computadora** = computer (Latin America); in Spain: **el ordenador**. Both are correct.
Related: **la tienda** (store), **el precio** (price), **la oferta** (sale/offer), **las compras** (shopping).
cards.englishPhrase: I need to buy a new computer.

cards.grammarNote:
**Ayudar** = to help (a regular -ar verb).
**¿Puedo ayudarte?** — **ayudarte** is an infinitive with a clitic pronoun attached: **ayudar** + **te** (you).
This is called an "attached pronoun" on an infinitive. Alternatively: **¿Te puedo ayudar?** (same meaning, pronoun before the conjugated verb).
**Puedo** = I can — from **poder** (o→ue stem-changer): **puedo, puedes, puede...**
**Ayudar a** + person: **Te ayudo a encontrarlo** (I'll help you find it).

**Dirigir** = to manage / to direct / to lead (an -ir verb).
Irregular yo form: **dirijo** (not *dirigo*) — the **g** changes to **j** before **o** to preserve the soft sound.
Full present: **dirijo, diriges, dirige, dirigimos, dirigís, dirigen**.
Related: **el director / la directora** (director/manager), **la dirección** (management/direction/address).
Alternatives for "to manage": **gestionar** (to manage/administer), **administrar** (to administer).

**Reunirse** = to meet/gather (a reflexive verb).
Reflexive pronouns: **me reúno, te reúnes, se reúne, nos reunimos, os reunís, se reúnen**.
Note the accent: **reúno, reúnes, reúne, reúnen** — the stress falls on the **ú** in most forms (but NOT in nosotros/vosotros).
**Nos reunimos** = we meet — note no accent here (stress on **ni** is regular).
**Cada lunes** = every Monday — **cada** (each/every) + singular: **cada día**, **cada semana**, **cada mes**.

**Empezar** is a stem-changing verb (e→ie): **empiezo, empiezas, empieza, empezamos, empezáis, empiezan**.
Note: no stem change in **nosotros/vosotros** forms.
**Empezar a + infinitive** = to start doing something: **empiezo a trabajar** (I start working).
Note also the spelling change: **z → c** before **e** in preterite: **empecé** (I started).
Synonym: **comenzar** (identical conjugation pattern — also e→ie).
cards.phrase: Empiezo a trabajar a las ocho.

cards.grammarNote:
**Terminar** = to finish / to end (a regular -ar verb).
**Terminar de + infinitive** = to finish doing something: **termino de trabajar** (I finish working), **terminé de comer** (I finished eating).
Compare: **terminar** (to finish) vs. **empezar** (to start) — natural opposites.
**A las cinco** = at five (o'clock) — telling time: **a la una** (at one), **a las dos/tres...** (at two/three...).
cards.phrase: Termino de trabajar a las cinco.

cards.grammarNote:
**gustar** + infinitive = to like doing something
**Me gusta leer** (I like reading) · **A ella le gusta cantar** (She likes singing)
For clarity with third-person subjects, add **a** + person: **A mi padre le gusta pescar**
**gustar** agrees with what is liked, not the person doing the liking
cards.englishPhrase: I like reading. She likes singing.
cards.phrase: Me gusta leer. A ella le gusta cantar.

cards.grammarNote:
**Relajarse** is a reflexive verb: **me relajo, te relajas, se relaja, nos relajamos...**
**Me relajo** = I relax — the reflexive **me** shows the action reflects back on the subject.
Reflexive verbs for mental/physical states are very common in Spanish: **relajarse** (to relax), **distraerse** (to get distracted), **concentrarse** (to focus), **aburrirse** (to get bored).
**Los fines de semana** = on weekends — **los** + time noun expresses recurrence.
cards.phrase: Me relajo los fines de semana.

cards.grammarNote:
**Estresante** is another invariable adjective (ending in **-ante**): **un trabajo estresante** / **una situación estresante** — same form for masculine and feminine.
Borrowed from English "stress" → **estrés** (noun, masculine: **el estrés**) → **estresante** (adjective) → **estresarse** (reflexive verb: to get stressed).
Use **ser** for a job's inherent quality: **Mi trabajo es estresante**.
Contrast with **estar estresado/a** (to feel stressed right now — a temporary state).

Adverb form: **felizmente** (happily) — add **-mente** to the feminine adjective
**feliz** has no gender change: feliz + mente → **felizmente** · **Ella sonrió felizmente.**
Adverb form: **tristemente** (sadly) — **triste** has no gender change: triste + mente → **tristemente** · **Habló tristemente.**

**amor** comes from Latin **amor** (love, desire) — the same root as English *amorous*.
Verb forms: **amar** (to love deeply), **querer** (to love/want — more everyday).
**Te quiero** (I love you — common between family/friends) vs **Te amo** (I love you — more intense/romantic).
cards.englishPhrase: I feel a lot of love for my family.
cards.phrase: Siento mucho amor por mi familia.

cards.grammarNote:
**enojo** = anger, annoyance — the most common everyday word across Latin America.
**enfado** is more common in Spain.
**ira** = wrath/rage — strong and formal, from Latin. You'd use it in writing or when describing intense anger.
**Me dio enojo** = it made me angry (lit. "it gave me anger") — **dar** is commonly used this way: **me da risa** (it makes me laugh), **me da miedo** (it scares me).
cards.englishPhrase: It made me angry when they lied to me.
cards.phrase: Me dio enojo cuando me mintieron.

cards.grammarNote:
**tener miedo** = to be afraid (literally *to have fear*) — Spanish uses **tener** + noun for many states.
**tener miedo de/a + infinitive**: **tengo miedo de caer** (I'm afraid of falling).
Also: **dar miedo** = to frighten — **me da miedo** (it frightens me / it scares me).

**esperanza** (hope) is a noun; the verb is **esperar** (to hope, to wait, to expect).
Note the suffix **-anza** forming abstract nouns: **confianza** (trust), **enseñanza** (teaching), **esperanza** (hope).
**Espero que + subjunctive**: **espero que todo salga bien** (I hope everything goes well).
cards.englishPhrase: I have hope for the future.

cards.grammarNote:
**estrés** is a borrowed word from English *stress* — note the accent on the final syllable.
The adjective is **estresado/a** (stressed): **estoy estresado** (I'm stressed) — uses **estar** for the temporary state.
Also: **estresante** (stressful) — **un trabajo estresante** (a stressful job).
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of stress at work.
cards.phrase: Tengo mucho estrés en el trabajo.

cards.grammarNote:
**estado de ánimo** = mood (literally *state of spirit/soul*).
**ánimo** alone means spirit, cheer, courage — **¡Ánimo!** = Cheer up! / Come on!
Also common: **estar de buen humor** (to be in a good mood) and **estar de mal humor** (to be in a bad mood).
cards.englishPhrase: I'm in a good mood today.
cards.phrase: Hoy estoy de buen estado de ánimo.

cards.grammarNote:
**sentimiento** (feeling, emotion) comes from **sentir** (to feel).
The suffix **-miento** forms nouns from verbs: **sentir → sentimiento**, **conocer → conocimiento** (knowledge), **pensar → pensamiento** (thought).
Also related: **sentido** = sense (as in the five senses, or *meaning*).

**emoción** = emotion, but also *excitement* — context determines the meaning.
The verb **emocionar** = to move emotionally / to excite: **me emociona** (it moves me / it excites me).
Reflexive **emocionarse** = to get emotional: **se emocionó** (he/she got emotional / teared up).

**calma** (noun) = calm, calmness.
Adjective form: **tranquilo/a** or **calmado/a** (calm, relaxed).
Use **estar** for the temporary state: **estoy tranquilo** (I'm calm right now) vs **soy tranquilo** (I'm a calm person by nature).
Also: **mantener la calma** (to keep calm) — a very common phrase.

**preocupación** (worry, concern) — noun from **preocupar** (to worry/concern).
The reflexive **preocuparse** = to worry oneself: **me preocupo** (I worry), **no te preocupes** (don't worry).
The suffix **-ción** forms feminine nouns from verbs: **preocupar → preocupación**, **emocionar → emoción**.
cards.phrase: No dejes que la preocupación te detenga.

cards.grammarNote:
**sorpresa** (surprise) — from **sorprender** (to surprise).
**¡Qué sorpresa!** = What a surprise! — the **¡Qué + noun!** structure expresses exclamation.
Adjective: **sorprendido/a** (surprised) — use **estar**: **estoy sorprendido** (I'm surprised).
Also: **me sorprendió** (it surprised me) — verb used like **gustar** with indirect object pronouns.

**odio** = hate (noun) — also the yo form of **odiar** (to hate): **yo odio** (I hate).
Note that **odio** as a noun takes a definite article: **el odio es destructivo** (hate is destructive).
Compare: **ira** (wrath/anger — more formal), **rencor** (resentment, grudge), **enojo** (everyday anger).
cards.phrase: El odio es un sentimiento fuerte.

cards.grammarNote:
**dolor** (pain) — from Latin **dolor**, same root as English *dolorous*.
**tener dolor de + body part**: **tengo dolor de cabeza** (I have a headache), **tengo dolor de estómago** (I have a stomachache).
Verb: **doler** (to hurt/ache) — works like **gustar**: **me duele la cabeza** (my head hurts — lit. the head hurts me).
cards.englishPhrase: I feel pain in my leg.

cards.grammarNote:
**energía** (energy) — note the accent on the **í** (énfasis on the third syllable from the end).
**tener energía** = to have energy — using **tener** for states: **tengo mucha energía** (I have a lot of energy).
Adjective: **enérgico/a** (energetic) — use **ser** for a personality trait: **es muy enérgico** (he's very energetic).
cards.englishPhrase: I have a lot of energy today.

cards.grammarNote:
**sentir** = to feel/perceive something · **sentirse** (reflexive) = to feel a certain way
**Me siento bien** (I feel good) · **Siento dolor** (I feel pain)

**amar** = to love (deeply, often romantic or profound love).
Compare **querer** = to love/want — more versatile and common in everyday speech: **te quiero** (I love you) is used between family and close friends.
**Te amo** is more intense and typically romantic; **te quiero** is warmer and more common day-to-day.

**odiar** = to hate — a regular -ar verb: **odio, odias, odia, odiamos, odiáis, odian**.
**odiar + infinitive** = to hate doing something: **odio esperar** (I hate waiting), **odia llegar tarde** (he hates being late).
Less intense alternatives: **no soportar** (can't stand), **detestar** (to detest).

**gustar** works opposite to English — the subject is what is liked, not the person.
**Me gusta la música** = Music pleases me (I like music).
Indirect object pronouns: **me** (to me), **te** (to you), **le** (to him/her), **nos** (to us), **les** (to them).
**Me gustan** (plural) vs **me gusta** (singular): **me gustan los libros** (I like books).

**disfrutar** = to enjoy — can take **de** or a direct object: **disfrutar de la vida** or **disfrutar la vida**.
Both are correct; **disfrutar de** is slightly more formal.
Also reflexive: **disfrutarse** is used in some Latin American countries — **¡disfrútalo!** (enjoy it!).

**tener miedo** = to be afraid / to be scared (lit. "to have fear") — the most natural everyday expression.
**Me da miedo** = it scares me (lit. "it gives me fear") — very common: **me da miedo volar** (flying scares me).
**temer** = to fear — a regular -er verb but formal/literary. You'd see it in writing more than speech.
**miedoso/a** = scaredy-cat / easily scared (adjective).

**esperar** has three meanings: to hope, to wait, and to expect.
**esperar que + subjunctive** = to hope that: **espero que todo salga bien** (I hope everything goes well).
**esperar a + infinitive** = to wait to do something: **espero a ver** (I'll wait and see).
Context clarifies which meaning is intended — often all three blend together.

**preocuparse** is a reflexive verb — to worry oneself.
Full conjugation: **me preocupo, te preocupas, se preocupa, nos preocupamos**.
**No te preocupes** = Don't worry — the **te** is the reflexive pronoun (tú form).
Non-reflexive **preocupar** = to worry someone else: **me preocupa** (it worries me / I'm worried about it).

**paz** (peace) — from Latin **pax** (same root as English *pacify*, *pacific*).
Note the plural: **paces** (though rarely used). The phrase **hacer las paces** = to make peace / to make up.
**tranquilidad** (quiet, tranquility) is a close synonym — **necesito paz y tranquilidad** (I need peace and quiet).
**celos** is typically plural · **tener celos** = to be jealous · **envidia** = envy (wanting what someone else has)

**molestar** = to bother, to annoy — works like **gustar**: the annoying thing is the subject.
**Ese ruido me molesta** = That noise bothers me (lit. that noise molests/disturbs me).
Reflexive **molestarse** = to be bothered / to take the trouble: **no te molestes** (don't bother).
Note: **molestar** is not as strong as English *molest* — it simply means to disturb or annoy.

**enojar** = to anger (someone else) — transitive: **ese comentario me enojó** (that comment angered me).
Reflexive **enojarse** = to get angry: **me enojé** (I got angry), **se enoja fácilmente** (he gets angry easily).
**ponerse enojado/a** = to become angry — **se puso enojada** (she became angry).
Note: **enojado** uses **estar** — **estoy enojado** (I'm angry right now).

**sonreír** = to smile — a compound of **son-** (sound/tone) + **reír** (to laugh).
**sonreír** is an irregular e→i stem-changing verb: **sonrío, sonríes, sonríe, sonreímos, sonreís, sonríen**.
Noun: **la sonrisa** (the smile) — **tiene una sonrisa hermosa** (she has a beautiful smile).
Note the written accent on **sonríe** to separate the two vowels.

**reír** = to laugh — irregular e→i stem-changing verb: **río, ríes, ríe, reímos, reís, ríen**.
Reflexive **reírse** is also common and essentially interchangeable: **nos reímos** (we laughed).
**reírse de** = to laugh at: **se ríen de mí** (they're laughing at me).
Noun: **la risa** (the laugh, laughter) — **me dio risa** (it made me laugh).

**llorar** = to cry — a regular -ar verb: **lloro, lloras, llora, lloramos, lloráis, lloran**.
The present progressive **está llorando** (is crying) uses **estar** + gerund (-ando/-iendo).
**hacerse llorar** = to make someone cry: **me hizo llorar** (it made me cry).
Note: **llover** (to rain) sounds similar but is unrelated — **llueve** (it's raining).

**gritar** = to shout, to scream — a regular -ar verb.
**No grites** = Don't shout — negative tú command: use the present subjunctive (**grites**).
Noun: **el grito** (the shout, scream) — **un grito de alegría** (a cry of joy), **a voces / a gritos** (shouting, at the top of one's voice).
Also: **dar un grito** = to let out a shout.

**relajarse** is a reflexive verb — to relax (oneself).
**Relájate** = Relax! — affirmative tú command of the reflexive: drop **-s** from **te relajas**, then attach **-te**: **relájate** (note the accent to preserve stress).
Full conjugation: **me relajo, te relajas, se relaja, nos relajamos**.
Also: **estar relajado/a** = to be relaxed (state) — **estoy muy relajado** (I'm very relaxed).
Adverb form: **enojadamente** (angrily) — feminine: enojada + mente → **enojadamente** · **Respondió enojadamente.**

**asustado/a** = scared, frightened — past participle of **asustar** (to frighten) used as an adjective.
Always use **estar**: **estaba asustado** (he was scared) — a temporary emotional state.
Verb: **asustarse** (reflexive) = to get scared: **me asusté** (I got scared), **no te asustes** (don't get scared).
Also: **tener miedo** (to be afraid) and **asustado** often overlap — **tenía miedo** vs **estaba asustado**.
Adverb form: **ansiosamente** (anxiously) — feminine: ansiosa + mente → **ansiosamente** · **Esperaba ansiosamente.**
Adverb form: **nerviosamente** (nervously) — feminine: nerviosa + mente → **nerviosamente** · **Habló nerviosamente.**
Adverb form: **emocionadamente** (excitedly) — feminine: emocionada + mente → **emocionadamente** · **Gritó emocionadamente.**

**alegre** (joyful, cheerful) — from Latin **alacer** (lively, brisk), the same root as **alegría** (joy).
The suffix **-ía** forms abstract nouns: **alegre → alegría** (joy), **cortés → cortesía** (courtesy).
Note the use of **estar**: **siempre está alegre** (she's always cheerful) — even with *siempre*, **estar** is used because it describes a perceived/observed state.
**ponerse alegre** = to become cheerful/tipsy — **me pongo alegre con el vino** (wine makes me happy/tipsy).
Adverb form: **orgullosamente** (proudly) — feminine: orgullosa + mente → **orgullosamente** · **Sonrió orgullosamente.**

**contento/a** = content, happy, pleased — always use **estar**: **estoy contento** (I'm content/pleased).
Do not confuse with **contento** as a noun (rarely used) or **contenido** (content, as in the content of a book).
**sentirse contento** = to feel content: **me siento contento con mi vida** (I feel content with my life).
Related: **satisfecho/a** (satisfied) — **estoy satisfecho** (I'm satisfied).
Adverb form: **tranquilamente** (calmly) — feminine: tranquila + mente → **tranquilamente** · **Respondió tranquilamente.**

**estresado/a** = stressed — past participle of **estresar** used as an adjective.
Always use **estar**: **estoy muy estresado** (I'm very stressed) — a temporary state, not a permanent personality trait.
**ponerse estresado** = to become stressed: **me pongo estresado cuando hay mucho trabajo** (I get stressed when there's a lot of work).
The noun **estrés** is a loanword from English — note the accent on the final syllable.

**abrumado/a** = overwhelmed — from **abrumar** (to overwhelm, to weigh down).
**sentirse abrumado** uses the reflexive **sentirse**: **me siento abrumado** (I feel overwhelmed).
Use **estar** for the resulting state: **estoy abrumado** (I'm overwhelmed).
The preposition **por** marks the cause: **abrumado por el trabajo** (overwhelmed by the work).
cards.englishPhrase: I feel overwhelmed by the work.
cards.phrase: Me siento abrumado por el trabajo.

cards.grammarNote:
**energético/a** = energetic — adjective from **energía** (energy).
Use **ser** for a personality trait: **es muy energética** (she's very energetic by nature).
Contrast with **estar lleno/a de energía** (to be full of energy — a current state): **hoy estoy lleno de energía**.
Note gender agreement: **energético** (masculine), **energética** (feminine).
Adverb form: **cansadamente** (wearily) — feminine: cansada + mente → **cansadamente** · **Arrastró los pies cansadamente.**

**agotado/a** = exhausted, depleted — from **agotar** (to exhaust, to drain, to use up).
Always use **estar**: **estoy agotado** (I'm exhausted) — a temporary physical/emotional state.
**agotado** can also mean *sold out*: **las entradas están agotadas** (the tickets are sold out) — same verb, different context.
**agotador/a** = exhausting: **fue un día agotador** (it was an exhausting day).

**curioso/a** = curious — can describe a person or a thing (meaning *strange/interesting*).
Use **estar** for the current emotional state: **estoy curioso por eso** (I'm curious about that).
Use **ser** for personality: **es una persona muy curiosa** (she's a very curious person).
Also: **tener curiosidad** = to be curious: **tengo mucha curiosidad por saber** (I'm very curious to know).

**doler** (to hurt) works like **gustar** — the body part is the grammatical subject
**Me duele la cabeza** (singular) · **Me duelen los pies** (plural)
The pronoun **me/te/le** indicates who is hurting

**el pelo** is the everyday word for hair (on the head); **el cabello** is more formal/literary.
In the phrase **Ella tiene el pelo largo**, the definite article **el** is used instead of a possessive — Spanish describes physical characteristics this way: **tiene los ojos azules** (she has blue eyes), **tiene la nariz pequeña** (he has a small nose).

**Lávate la cara** is a reflexive command (tú form): **lávate** = wash yourself.
With body-care reflexive verbs, use the **definite article** (**la cara**, **las manos**) not a possessive (**tu cara**).
The reflexive pronoun **te** already shows whose face it is.
Formal command (usted): **Lávese la cara**.

Paired body parts use the plural with the definite article: **los ojos** (eyes), **las manos** (hands), **los pies** (feet), **los oídos** (ears).
Spanish describes eye color with **tener + los + body part + adjective**: **Él tiene los ojos azules** — literally 'he has the eyes blue.' The adjective follows the noun and agrees in gender and number.

Spanish has two words for ear: **la oreja** (the outer, visible ear) and **el oído** (the inner ear / sense of hearing).
**Me duele la oreja** = my outer ear hurts · **Tengo el oído tapado** = my inner ear is blocked.
**doler** works like **gustar**: the body part is the subject, **me** is the indirect object pronoun.

**Tengo la nariz fría** uses **tener + definite article + body part + adjective** to describe a physical state.
This pattern is very common: **tengo el cuello rígido** (my neck is stiff), **tengo la pierna cansada** (my leg is tired).
Contrast with **me duele** for pain: **me duele la nariz** (my nose hurts).

**Abre la boca** is an informal (tú) imperative. Regular -ar verbs form the tú command with the él/ella present form: **abr-e**.
The formal (usted) command is **Abra la boca** — note the vowel switch: -ar verbs use -e for formal commands.
Note the definite article **la** — not *tu boca*.

Paired body parts use the plural with definite article: **los labios** (lips), not *sus labios* when describing a person's physical features.
**Tiene los labios rojos** — the adjective **rojos** agrees in gender (masculine) and number (plural) with **labios**.
This **tener + los/las + body part + adjective** structure describes physical appearance.

**doler** works like **gustar** — the tooth is the grammatical subject: **Me duele un diente** (a tooth is hurting me).
Note **un** (indefinite article) instead of **el** here — 'a tooth' (one in particular, but not previously specified).
For general toothache: **tener dolor de muelas** (to have a toothache) — **muela** refers specifically to a molar.

**la lengua** means both 'tongue' (body part) and 'language' in Spanish: **hablar una lengua** (to speak a language).
**Saca la lengua** — **sacar** (to take out / stick out) is an informal tú command. Note the definite article **la** instead of a possessive.
For the formal command: **Saque la lengua**.

**el cuello** means both 'neck' (body part) and 'collar/neckline' of a garment.
**Tengo el cuello rígido** uses **tener + el + body part + adjective** for physical states.
For pain: **Me duele el cuello** (my neck hurts) using the **doler** + gustar pattern.
**rígido** (stiff/rigid) agrees in gender with **cuello** (masculine).

**Me rompí el brazo** — reflexive verb (**romper** → **romperse**) with the definite article, not a possessive.
The reflexive pronoun **me** shows it's my own arm; **el** replaces *mi*.
This pattern applies to all injury verbs: **me torcí el tobillo** (I sprained my ankle), **me corté el dedo** (I cut my finger).
**rompí** is preterite (past): **romper** → rompí, rompiste, rompió, rompimos, rompieron.

With reflexive verbs and body parts, use the definite article instead of a possessive:
**Lávate las manos** (not *lava tus manos*) · **Me rompí el brazo** (I broke my arm)
The reflexive pronoun **me/te/se** makes clear whose body part it is

Spanish uses **el dedo** for both finger and toe. To distinguish:
**el dedo de la mano** (finger) · **el dedo del pie** (toe).
**Se cortó el dedo** — reflexive **cortarse** (to cut oneself) with definite article instead of possessive.
The reflexive pronoun **se** shows it was his own finger; **el** replaces *su*.

**tener dolor en** + body part = to have pain in a body part: **tiene dolor en el pecho** (he has chest pain).
Alternative: **tener dolor de** + body part for common ailments: **dolor de cabeza** (headache), **dolor de espalda** (back pain), **dolor de estómago** (stomachache).
**el pecho** can also refer to the breast area generally; **el seno** is more specific for breast.
cards.phrase: Él tiene dolor en el pecho.

cards.grammarNote:
**doler** works like **gustar**: **Me duele la espalda** — literally 'the back hurts to me.'
For specific regions: **la parte baja de la espalda** (lower back) · **la parte alta de la espalda** (upper back).
Common compound: **dolor de espalda** (back pain) — used with **tener**: **tengo dolor de espalda**.

**doler** works like **gustar**: **Me duele el hombro** — literally 'the shoulder hurts to me.'
Common expressions: **encogerse de hombros** (to shrug — literally 'to shrink from the shoulders') · **cargar con algo sobre los hombros** (to carry something on one's shoulders — literal and figurative).
For injury: **me hice daño en el hombro** or **me lesioné el hombro** (I hurt my shoulder).

**Se golpeó el codo** — reflexive **golpearse** (to bump/hit oneself) with definite article.
The reflexive **se** shows the action happened to his own body; **el** replaces *su*.
**el codo** also appears in the idiom **hablar por los codos** (to talk someone's ear off — literally 'to talk through the elbows').
For pain: **me duele el codo** (my elbow hurts) — **doler** + gustar pattern.

**la rodilla** comes from Latin **rotella** (little wheel) — referring to the round kneecap. Related medical term: **la rótula** (kneecap/patella).
**Me lastimé la rodilla** — reflexive **lastimarse** (to hurt oneself) with definite article instead of possessive.
Alternative: **me hice daño en la rodilla** (I hurt myself on the knee) — **hacerse daño en** + body part is a very common injury expression.

**Tengo la pierna cansada** — **tener + la + body part + adjective** for physical states.
The adjective **cansada** agrees in gender (feminine) with **la pierna**.
For pain: **Me duele la pierna** (my leg hurts) — using the **doler** + gustar pattern.
Paired form: **tengo las piernas cansadas** (my legs are tired) — plural adjective agrees with plural noun.

Paired body parts use the plural: **los pies** (feet) — **Me duelen los pies** (my feet hurt).
**doler** agrees with the plural subject: **me duele** (singular) · **me duelen** (plural).
Common expression: **estar de pie** (to be standing) · **ponerse de pie** (to stand up) · **a pie** (on foot).

**el dedo del pie** (toe) — **del** is a contraction of **de + el**. This distinguishes toe from finger (**el dedo de la mano**).
**Se golpeó el dedo del pie** — reflexive **golpearse** with definite article: the reflexive **se** shows it was his own toe.
**golpear** (to hit/strike) → **golpearse** (to hit/bang oneself). Preterite: **golpeó**.
cards.phrase: Se golpeó el dedo del pie.

cards.grammarNote:
**doler** works like **gustar**: **Me duele el estómago** — the stomach is the grammatical subject.
Common alternatives: **tener dolor de estómago** · **tener el estómago revuelto** (to have an upset stomach).
Note: **el estómago** (stomach organ) vs. **el vientre/la barriga** (belly, more colloquial).

**El cuerpo humano es asombroso** — **ser** is used (**es**) because this describes an inherent, permanent quality.
**asombroso** (amazing/astonishing) comes from **asombrar** (to astonish) — related to English 'umbra' (shadow), from the idea of being 'overshadowed' by awe.
**el cuerpo** appears in many expressions: **en cuerpo y alma** (body and soul) · **a cuerpo de rey** (in the lap of luxury — literally 'at a king's body') · **hacer del cuerpo** (to go to the bathroom, euphemistic).

**corazón** comes from Latin **cor** (heart) — the same root as English 'courage,' 'cordial,' 'core,' and 'accord.'
**late** (beats/throbs) comes from **latir** — used specifically for heartbeat: **el corazón late rápido**.
Note the possessive **Mi corazón** here — used because this is a statement about the subject's own heart without a reflexive verb.

**Me jalé un músculo** — **jalarse** (to pull, strain) is primarily used in Latin America; in Spain the equivalent is **me estiré un músculo**.
The reflexive **me** shows the action happened to the speaker's own body; **un** (not **el**) because it's 'a muscle' — one unspecified one.
For generalized soreness: **tengo los músculos doloridos** (my muscles are sore).

**Ella tiene la piel suave** — **tener + la + body part + adjective** for physical descriptions.
**la piel** (skin) also means leather/hide — a shared literal meaning: **una chaqueta de piel** (a leather jacket).
With **estar**: **estar en la piel de alguien** = to be in someone's shoes (idiomatic).
**suave** is invariable for gender — same form for masculine and feminine.

**la sangre** (blood) is feminine — used without article after **donar**: **donó sangre** (donated blood), like **donar tiempo** (to donate time).
Related vocabulary: **sangrar** (to bleed) · **el análisis de sangre** (blood test) · **la presión arterial** (blood pressure).
**sangriento** (bloody) and **ensangrentado** (bloodied) are common adjectives.

**cerebro** comes from Latin **cerebrum** — directly related to English 'cerebral' and 'cerebellum' (the little brain).
With **ser** (permanent characteristic): **El cerebro es complejo** — use **ser** for inherent properties of things.
Contrast: **estar** would suggest a temporary state — **el cerebro está activo** (the brain is [currently] active).

**el seno** (breast) — also used in the plural **los senos**. **el pecho** is used more broadly for chest/breast area.
**sintió** is the preterite of **sentir** (to feel) — an e→i stem-changing verb in the preterite: **sentí, sentiste, sintió, sentimos, sentisteis, sintieron**.
**tener dolor en** + body part: **tuvo dolor en el pecho** (she had chest pain).
cards.englishPhrase: She felt pain in her chest.
cards.phrase: Ella sintió dolor en el pecho.

cards.grammarNote:
**ver** (to see) is irregular in the present: **veo, ves, ve, vemos, veis, ven**.
**Puedo ver con claridad** — **poder + infinitive** (can/to be able to + verb).
**poder** is an o→ue stem-changer: **puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, podéis, pueden**.
Distinction: **ver** (to see, passive perception) vs. **mirar** (to look at, active attention): **Mira** ese pájaro · **Veo** la luna.

Spanish has two verbs for hearing: **oír** (to hear, passive) and **escuchar** (to listen, active).
The phrase uses **escucho** — 'I'm not listening to you / I can't hear you' (active attention).
**No te escucho** — **te** is an indirect object pronoun here ('you' as the one being heard).
**oír** is highly irregular: **oigo, oyes, oye, oímos, oís, oyen**.

**oler** (to smell) is an o→hue stem-changing verb — uniquely, it adds an **h** before the diphthong: **huelo, hueles, huele, olemos, oléis, huelen**.
This spelling preserves the /w/ sound — Spanish doesn't begin a syllable with 'ue' without 'h' when it could be confused.
**Puedo oler las flores** — **poder + infinitive** for ability.

Two verbs for tasting: **saborear** (to savor, taste slowly) and **probar** (to taste/try).
The phrase uses **Prueba** (try/taste this) — an informal tú command of **probar** (o→ue stem-changer).
**probar** also means 'to try on' (clothing) and 'to prove': **¿Probaste el vestido?** (Did you try on the dress?)
**saborear** is from **sabor** (flavor/taste) — related to 'savor' in English.

**¡No toques eso!** — **toques** is the negative tú subjunctive command (present subjunctive) of **tocar**.
Negative tú commands always use the present subjunctive: **no hables, no comas, no toques**.
**tocar** has a spelling change in the subjunctive: c→qu before **e** to preserve the /k/ sound: **toque, toques, toque**.
**tocar** also means 'to play' (an instrument): **toco la guitarra**.

**Respira despacio** — informal (tú) imperative of **respirar** (regular -ar verb): drop the -r and the form is identical to the third-person present.
Formal command: **Respire despacio** — note vowel switch (-ar → -e ending for usted).
**despacio** (slowly) is an adverb — invariable, never changes form.
Related: **la respiración** (breathing/respiration) · **respiratorio** (respiratory).

**Dobla las rodillas** — informal (tú) imperative of **doblar** (regular -ar).
**la rodilla** (knee) comes from Latin **rotella** (little wheel) — the kneecap's circular shape. Related English cognate: 'rotella' → 'rotula' (medical term for kneecap).
Note definite article **las** instead of possessive — 'bend the knees' (understood as yours).
**doblar** also means 'to fold,' 'to turn' (a corner), and 'to dub' (a film).

**Estira los brazos** — informal (tú) imperative of **estirar** (regular -ar).
Note **los brazos** (the arms) with definite article, not *tus brazos*.
**estirar** vs. **extender**: **estirar** suggests pulling/stretching something out; **extender** (to extend/spread) is used for more formal contexts.
Related: **el estiramiento** (the stretch/stretching) · **estirarse** (to stretch oneself — reflexive).

**Sudo cuando corro** — both verbs are present tense, expressing habitual action (I sweat [whenever] I run).
Spanish uses present indicative in **cuando** clauses for habitual/repeated events.
Contrast: for future events, **cuando** takes the subjunctive: **Cuando corra mañana, sudaré** (When I run tomorrow, I'll sweat).
**sudar** (to sweat) · **el sudor** (sweat/perspiration) · **sudoroso** (sweaty).

**¿Cómo te sientes?** uses **sentirse** (reflexive) for emotional/physical feeling: **me siento bien** (I feel well).
Contrast with non-reflexive **sentir** (to feel/sense something): **Siento un dolor** (I feel a pain).
**sentirse** conjugates like a reflexive: **me siento, te sientes, se siente, nos sentimos, os sentís, se sienten**.
**sentir** is an e→ie stem-changer in the present: **siento, sientes, siente**.

**pensar** is an e→ie stem-changing verb — changes in all forms except nosotros/vosotros:
**pienso · piensas · piensa · pensamos · pensáis · piensan**
Other e→ie verbs: **querer** (quiero) · **entender** (entiendo) · **empezar** (empiezo) · **perder** (pierdo)

**mover** is an o→ue stem-changing verb: **muevo, mueves, mueve, movemos, movéis, mueven**.
**No puedo mover el brazo** — note **el brazo** (the arm) with definite article, not *mi brazo*.
**poder** (can/to be able to) is also o→ue: **puedo, puedes, puede**.
Reflexive **moverse** = to move (oneself): **No puedo moverme** (I can't move).

**suave** is invariable for gender — same form for masculine and feminine: **el tejido suave** / **la piel suave**.
**ser** vs. **estar** with **suave**: **El tejido es suave** (the tissue is soft — inherent property, use **ser**) vs. **El tejido está suave** (the tissue feels soft — current/perceived state, use **estar**).
Related: **suavidad** (softness) · **suavizar** (to soften) · **suavemente** (softly, gently).

**Tengo los músculos doloridos** — **tener + los + body part (plural) + adjective** for physical states.
**dolorido** (sore/aching) comes from **dolor** (pain) — related to **doler** (to hurt) and **doloroso** (painful).
The adjective **doloridos** agrees in gender (masculine) and number (plural) with **los músculos**.
Common after exercise: **tengo las piernas doloridas** (my legs are sore).

**izquierdo/izquierda** (left) comes from Basque **ezker** — one of the few Basque loanwords in Spanish.
Adjectives of direction follow the noun: **la rodilla izquierda** (the left knee), **el brazo derecho** (the right arm).
**izquierda** agrees in gender (feminine) with **la rodilla**.
Common expressions: **a la izquierda** (to the left) · **de izquierdas** (left-wing, politically).

**derecho/derecha** (right direction) also means 'straight' and 'right' (legal/moral): **los derechos humanos** (human rights), **ir derecho** (to go straight).
**Me rompí el brazo derecho** — reflexive injury pattern with definite article: the **me** shows whose arm, so **el** not *mi*.
**derecho** agrees in gender (masculine) with **el brazo**.
Distinction: **derecho** (adjective, right/straight) vs. **a la derecha** (to the right — directional phrase).

**superior** is invariable for gender — same form for masculine and feminine nouns.
**la parte superior del cuerpo** — **del** is a contraction of **de + el**: *de el* → **del**.
**ser** is used here (**es fuerte**) because strength is an inherent characteristic of the upper body — not a temporary state.
Opposite: **inferior** (lower) — both are Latin-derived adjectives, same in English.
cards.phrase: La parte superior del cuerpo es fuerte.

cards.grammarNote:
**inferior** is invariable for gender — same form for masculine and feminine nouns.
**tener dolor en la parte inferior de la espalda** — note **en** (in/at) before the specific location; compare **tener dolor de espalda** (general back pain) without **en**.
**del** (de + el) is used for contractions, but here the article is **la** (feminine), so no contraction: **de la espalda**.
Opposite: **superior** (upper) — both invariable adjectives from Latin.
cards.phrase: Él tiene dolor en la parte inferior de la espalda.
